title: Simply Atrocious Technical Support
text:
I purchased 2 Echos as well as the matching Amazon subwoofer. The sound quality from these 3 speakers when playing music is actually pretty good. That said, buyer beware if you plan to use these speakers to play audio from your Fire Stick. The sound is so choppy and so delayed that it's almost impossible to understand what is being said and, at a minimum, it's too irritating and distracting to actually enjoy whatever you are watching.
Now, before I posted this review, I attempted to resolve the issue using Amazon's online chat support feature. Doing this was a complete nightmare. I ended up chatting with 6 different representatives, and each of those conversations ended with, "To help you in this case. I would have to transfer your chat to technical department that can resolve your issue. It'll just take a minute. Please stay connected." It wasn't until the last representative that I was told that the Echo speakers are not capable of playing audio from the Fire Stick. When I was told this, I was shocked, especially since I couldn't find anywhere within the description of these devices where it stated that the Echo speakers were not capable of playing audio from the Fire Stick.
Regardless, I was so irritated with the absolute atrocious level of support I was provided, I decided that I would send Jeff Bezos himself an email that included a copy of my chat session. In response, I received an email from Amazon's "Tech Support Executive Customer Relations". Once again, I described the issues and also included a copy of the chat session that I had previously participated in. After a couple of days, I was told, "we were able to notice that the connection between your echo devices and your Wi-Fi network is unstable. Restarting your device, modem, and/or router can often solve issues like this." And I was told that if I continued to experience problems, I should contact my "internet service provider". The main reason I'm going into this detail is because when their "engineers" supposedly noticed that the connection between my Echo devices and my wifi was "unstable", my Echo devices were already disconnected and back in the box to be returned.
I did however attempt one last time to follow their next round of instructions but unfortunately, I never heard back from Amazon.
My Echo devices and subwoofer are all being returned and, given the lack of technical support I received, will refrain from purchasing any Amazon brand products that are even the least bit technical.

title: Really want to give this 5 stars, but handshake issues and customer service lacking
text:
This is a great projector, especially if you are using it for gaming. I was so impressed with it, I ditched the TV entirely. It's super bright. Great response times. Enough features. I have Fire Stick, Chromecast, PS4, and a direct connect HDMI all connected. But...

It has handshake issues. This isn't the end of the world, but it does make it annoying enough that I reached to Optoma customer service to see if they had any resolutions. I ran across mentions of the issue in multiple reviews, including Projector Central. The main issue I'm having is with a direct connection to my MacBook, Thunderboldt to HDMI. It basically won't hold the picture, constantly flickering. I've tried multiple cables and converters, nothing works. Other reviews mention issues with the PS4 (I've had none) or other devices. I've had minor issues with the Chromecast, but not as much as the direct connection. I believe this is a firmware issue, not a hardware issue. Customer support basically brushed me off even after I sent them links to all the other references of the handshake issue. They suggested I send it in, since it's still under warranty.

I haven't made up my mind on what I'll do with the unit yet. I don't want to send it back in, since they'll probably send me a refurb. I just wish Optoma would recognize there is an issue and look into it. They say they have no reported handshake issues. Well, I'm reporting it.

That said, this is a great projector for the money. I looked long and hard before upgrading. I settled on this one mainly because of the brightness and gaming aspects.

title: Misleading and false - its Not 10awg wire and really is Aluminum wire with copper clad!!!!!!!
text: The title and description is a bit misleading at best, but really falsely describes the wire. The wire is in fact 12awg, not 10awg as described, it measures approximately 2mm as described; which is 12awg wire size. The wire should measure approximately 2.6mm for it to be10awg wire. This makes a huge difference when calculating for voltage drop and or current. The insulation is flexible, it has a silicone like feel, but it is tough and thick, the outside diameter and markings make the wire appear to be a 10awg wire; again, the dimensions make it 12awg! Also, be aware this is NOT copper wire, it is aluminum wire with a copper cladding. For those who don't know, copper cladding is essentially a coating, in this case it is aluminum wire that has been copper plated. It will NOT solder well, you should make your terminations/ connections using properly rated compression connections. Pay close attention when sizing for current, you need to treat this as aluminum wire because it is just that, aluminum, its just copper coated. Copper wire has a much higher current carrying capability than aluminum wire. BTW, if its not obvious, copper wire is typically priced a bit higher than aluminum wire, primarily because the copper raw material cost a bit more than the aluminum raw material!

text:

I know it is reviewed as being soft wide open and soft at 24mm on the edges. My copy was not sharp at at any focal length in anything but studio light and then at f13 from about 28-70mm. In blue and golden hour for landscapes, even at f13 the dynamic range was so bad, I could not get any quality shots. I just got back from a long weekend to Shenandoah National Park. All shots with this lens were way too soft for pro work and went straight to the pixel afterlife. I ended up using my Canon 24-70 L II with a metabones for almost all of the trip. title: Very strange input pinout and impedance structure: Left Hot/Right Hot/ Ground @ 20 K Ohms
text:
Product works BUT you need to have correct impedance and pinout feeding the Mic Input jack, otherwise, it is not a good fit.

After failing to get proper signal into device from standard Microphone output from Shure mixer, Tip/Ring/Sleeve = Hot/Minus/Ground, I contacted their tech support asking for the pinout and impedance of their mic input jack. To my suprise, the tech responded with "we can not give out internal wiring specifications". I totally lost it. I mean I am trying to figure out the most basic of things, namely what the pinout of my device should be in order to use their USB capture since it is NOT clearly specified in their literature and I get the "proprietary secret" response. As if I am trying to reverse engineer their precious device. Seriously? Like I said, I totally lost it.

After more back and forth, another tech support finally chimed in with the correct pinout for this device: Left Hot/ Right Hot/ Ground and high -z impedance. So I guess it is not a secret after all. I am not aware of any devices or microphones that actually put out such as signal, but I might be totally in the dark on this one as I don't really use consumer level mics which they say their capture device is built for. But that is the skinny folks . You need to have a device that outputs Unbalanced Stereo signal, but NOT at an unbalanced stereo signal line level of 600 ohms or even 10K ohms, but at a high-z impedance of 20K ohms. So you have to have a HIGH Z microphones that outputs a hot to both left and right channels (tip/ring) for this to work correctly. They keep saying "standard mic input" but sorry folks, there is nothing standard about a mic that feeds a hot to both tip and ring. That is a standard unbalanced line level pinout. So why not simply make it a line level device? Strange.

If you have a device that matches these specs, I am sure that this thing will work like a charm. If you don't, and don't want to mess around with impedance and line to mic level matching equipment, look around elsewhere for an Audio to USB capture device that takes in STANDARD MIC input of 150 ohms and that has a more realistic "standard" mic pinout of Hot/Minus/Ground for Tip/Ring/Sleeve (the Sabrent adapter for example).

I gave them two stars because they actually put up with my anger and insults after they initially insulted me with the "secret sauce" answer. They can play the high moral ground act, but if you insult someone with such audacious in your face snootiness, then you need to expect people to respond back in kind.

title: Terrible product until you file down the "sticking spot", Then GREAT!!!
text: There is basically only one left-handed wireless roller ball mouse on the market, the ELECOM M-XT4DRBK, and that's it! Nobody else seems to care about lefties. I am ambidextrous. I have two workstations: one with the Logitech right hand roller ball wireless mouse and I love it. Due to the way my two desks are set up, I use to use a wireless regular mouse with the left hand on my Leftie desk and the Logitech roller ball on my Rightie desk. Fatigue with a regular mouse on the Leftie made me look for a wireless lefty trackball mouse. One choice only......the Elecom. Everyone said the same thing-the ball sticks, jerks and the thing is basically unusable. You can clean the ball, swap balls with the Logitech or buy a replacement Logitech ball for $20 as some other reviewers suggested?? No way! Gotta be a better answer. Every time I used it, the mouse seems to glide well for a few strokes, then stick. Pulling out the ball revealed tiny bits of residue from the acrylic ball glazing on the support rollers inside. A careful examination of the ball and housing it sits in showed the upper circle arc gap was narrower on top than on the bottom, so the upper housing arc of plastic was rubbing on the ball, causing it to wear off the acrylic finish. The residue or worn off acrylic ended up on the 3 little rollers inside the cavity, but that wasn't enough to make the ball sticky and jerk. I sent the first one back thinking it was a problem with a deformed ball or housing and the replacement would be better. NOPE!!! .... same exact thing. Now I started thinking the receptacle opening for the ball needed closer examination because the tiny space between the housing and the ball was not uniform top to bottom. Filing off a tiny bit of plastic on the upper part of ball receptacle edge improved it some, but it was still sticking at odd times. After 3 more sessions of filing, testing, filing some more, I finally got the thing to work as smoothly as the Logitech. Then I swapped the balls back to their original owners to see if the ball was really the culprit. Nope, the balls work in both units. Seems to me a mouse that costs over $40 should not have to be FIXED by the purchaser to get it to work properly, but that's what it takes. I posted a picture with the yellow arrows pointing to the area to file down slowly and carefully so it works smoothly. Don't file away too much or the ball might fall out. Now you have a great left-handed wireless roller ball mouse!

title: Great speaker, but has some flaws. (Audiophile/Music Producer review)
text:
This speaker sounds great and has studio speaker quality sound, but it lacks the power that the Marshall Killburn II has. The bass response is good, but it lacks a lot of low end power, and the highs can get too loud.
The 52Hz bass response of the Marshall Killburn II vs the AudioPro Addon T3 60Hz bass response actually matters a lot when you are listening to music. It also makes the bass sound like they are on 15inch sub-woofers, compared to the AudioPro that sounds like mid-range speakers.

This speaker feels like something you would have sitting in a quiet office, while the Marshall Killburn II looks like some dj gear/dj speaker that is about to rock a party, and it has the power and bass response to prove it.

The highs get boosted at the loudest volumes, so it doesn't have that much power for bass. And while you are turning it up to almost max level, like level 7 8 9 and 10, the bass stays at a certain level while the highs keep getting louder and louder.
This speaker is at 25 watts, and the Marshall Killburn II is at 36 watts and sounds a lot louder and more powerful.
The Marshall Killburn II has knobs for volume, treble, and bass, that feels like dj decks, which this speaker really needs, but lacks. I was always listening to this speaker everyday wishing I could turn down the treble.
This speaker seems like a copy, and the Marshall Killburn II is the real deal.

Overall, it is a great sounding speaker that is really close to studio speaker quality. It's really great if you are listening to it at home, and in a quiet office environment and don't have to turn it up loud. But if you are going to be listening to music in a warehouse/outdoor environment, then I would recommend the Marshall Killburn II.

Also the FUGOO Tough XL sounds like blown;damaged midrange speakers if you were looking at that too...

title: Worth It, You Won't Be Sorry.  Don't Hesitate.
text:
In spit of using my laptop constantly (or so I thought), I never needed a laptop lift until the nationwide lockdown due to the Coronavirus. Working remotely thrust me into working online for 12-16 hours a day. After a week of that my neck was in so much pain, I didn't know how I was going to go on. I could no longer look down at my laptop without extreme pain, so I began looking down at my laptop for a solution on Amazon. I wanted something sturdy and easy to use without moving parts that could break and be annoying to adjust (preferably one pice). I liked this one because it seemed to have all the things I was looking for, and I like the silver-tone color. To be honest, there was one that I liked slightly more, but the projected delivery date was a week more than this one, and my neck couldn't take any more. Plus, this had many good reviews, and it weighted a bit more than the other one. For something that's going to support my MacBook Air, I prefer it to be heavier, and sturdier, so I ordered this one. I LOVE IT!
I'm trying to add pictures, but Amazon seems to have disabled that right now??? not sure, but i've added pictures to reviews in the past, but now I don't see that as an option.
Some reviewers complained that it's hard to adjust. It's not hard to adjust. It doesn't glide with the touch of a finger, no, but it's holding my MacBook Air. I wouldn't want it to be slipping up and down easily. It moves up and down stiffly, and yes, it does require a conscious effort and significant pressure. It's easier to adjust it without the laptop placed on it. I think this is the way we want the stand to be. It should take some effort to adjust it, so that it stays put. But it's not hard to get it to move the way you want it to go AT ALL. And, There are no separate parts that can get lost or broken. I love that.
My neck still hurts, because I'm on the computer just an unreasonable number of hours per day. But, my neck was to the point of no return before I got this, and without it, I couldn't have gone on, so this lift has really helped a lot.
I recommend ordering a separate keyboard and mouse so your hands can work comfortably below. It's not comfortable to raise your arms up so high to type. I knew this would be the case when I ordered this stand, so I also ordered an extra keyboard and mouse that I could use with the stand, to not have to raise my arms up high to type.
I saw one or more questions asking if it's uncomfortable to use the computer mousepad with the brackets projecting out from the stand. One reviewer said they're flush, so no, it isn't. They are absolutely NOT flush with my MacBook Air, however I don't think they would interfere with me using the mousepad, if I chose to use the laptop mousepad, which I sometimes do. Usually, however, I use the mouse and keyboard on the table level that I purchased.
If you're using a laptop for many hours a day, you should really invest in this lift. It's worth the money to help your neck and back, and to avoid headaches and neck/back pain. I've been using this lift for a couple of weeks, and I am very pleased with my purchase. I don't think you can go wrong with this lift.
One thing that could improve it a bit is to have the base be a little heavier. A couple of times it has started to tilt back a little. I have my keyboard on the base, which helps. A slightly heavier base would help more. No accidents so far with m MacBook Air toppling over, but still...

In addition, the card frequently disconnects when in close range and emits an alert, so the rate of false positive alerts when in advertised range is way too high.
So here is the sequence of events. The reconnection speed after getting in range is extremely slow. After entering a room and getting the red lack of connection signal, I wasn’t certain whether the wallet with card was located in another room or I should wait to see if it connected. So after waiting 2 minutes, I left and tried another room. Another 2 minute wait. After about 6 minutes I finally got the green connection signal. However, the sound from the wallet card was so low, that you need a quiet environment to hear it. Wouldn’t work for example in a public place or even most workplaces where ambient noise can’t be controlled. .Probably would also be difficult to hear if dropped between couch cushions.
The keychain locator fared better. The alert was louder and range was consistently better. Given the fact that wallet card was unreliable and hence unusable, I was left with deciding whether to keep the keychain locator (big and clunky also) or opt for one of the competitors.

title: A bit of a letdown, but still good
text:
I own Bose QC 35 wireless II headphones, and the Soundsport Wireless Free earbuds. Both pair simultaneously with with my smartphone and tablet through the Bose Connect app, so I rarely have to worry about connecting/disconnecting a device. My Soundsport Free’s battery finally died after two years. They are great earbuds...great fit, sound. So it was natural to order the new Bose Sport earbuds to replace them.

To my surprise, the new Sports required that I use the new “better” Bose Music app. Whatever it’s mysterious advantages, the new app will only connect the earbuds to one device at a time, so I have to swap the connection every time I switch between my smartphone and tablet. This is better? And I have to use two different apps for two Bluetooth wireless headphones from the same manufacturer? Makes no sense. Bose...it’s simple. One app that can control all your Bose wireless products...like Sonos. Really your current approach makes you look very second tier from a software perspective. Get with the program.

The Bose Sport earbuds don’t fit quite as well as the Soundsport Frees for me. I use the midsize tips, and they look to be the same size on both but on the Sports the material is a little stiffer and more grippy (intentional I’m sure), but this makes them have more pressure against the ear which is a little less comfortable than the Soundsports, but I don’t notice after a while and they are still comfortable, just not AS comfortable. All depends on your ears though, and they are light and will never fall out, and a great design overall IMHO.

The controls operate through touchpads on each earphone. People rightfully complained that there were no volume controls, but they added it to right earbud through a software update and it’s hit or miss but works okay when running, though very imprecise. The overall limited controls...no ability to skip back a track, but can skip forward, doesn’t really bother me, but maybe it does others. Overall I think the approach is to have fairly simple controls on the earbuds that you can operate without searching for a little button. I think it works overall, and once you get used to it you can execute basic controls without breaking a step - but you’ll still “miss” a lot. Oh...and a feature where if you take out the right earbud the music stops is actually very useful..a feature I can say really makes things easier for a runner like me seeing people I know on the street.

The sound is excellent, clean and deep bass (not “tight” or punchy) but accurate, with a wide soundstage with clear highs that you can play loud without hurting your ears. The sound doesn’t hit you up we the head with anything...just tries to present the whole picture accurately, and does this very well.

The phone capability is okay. Fine. No better than the Soundsport Free. Sometimes people can hear me and sometimes they can’t. Blech.

I’ve considered returning them, but for my use...mostly for running, working out and walking, they work well. Still pretty comfortable, very secure, good sound. Case is small enough for my needs but not svelte as many prefer. Battery life doesn’t compete well with competitors. There’s no reason Bose could not have added more charging hours in the larger case. What a miss competitively. But for me, 15 hours from a fully charged case and earbuds is plenty. There’s no noise cancellation...but I want to hear the cars coming. Not a need for me for this device.

The software thing really grates though. They need to add multipoint connectivity for this device via the app, and allow older devices to use the new Bose Music app. Like soon. They also should add some equalizer capability on the app.

Another weird thing. The bluetooth connectivity button is on the case, not the earbuds. Probably a way to make the earbudy ligher or simpler. BUT, as happened to me, if you go out or on a run and the earbuds are not connected to your device, there is no way to connect them without the case. I did the software update which disconnected them, then went on a run and by the time I realized this I was a half mile away and had to go without. Annoying. Im not sure what advantage this confers to the consumer. Maybe that's why the case is larger and doesnt have more battery supply. Who knows? I wish manufacturers would explain why they do things like this.

From a competitive feature standpoint, these earbuds don’t compare well with, say, Jabras, but if you appreciate the sound and comfortable, secure fit, you might end up preferring them anyway, especially as new software updates come out (I hope).

title: Suits my (weird?) needs as a hard limiter.
text:
When I called RDL, (or maybe it was email?) and explained what I wanted to do, they said that this microphone compressor might work but that they’d never tried it. It worked.

I’m in a band with punk singers who can’t be bothered to learn how to “work the mic“ by backing up when they sing loud (yell) which is often. We use a JamHub - which is awesome but esoteric and quirky. When the mic channels peak, the JamHub recordings (digital) skip. I was also worried about damaging it with frequent redlining. I initially got an Art preamp compressor but its xlr output is far too hot for the jamhub’s xlr inputs. I have to use it in the jamhub’s 1/4” ins (I don’t know whether it’s because the jamhub quarter inch trim is a lower level or because the preamp’s quarter-inch output is a lower level) which means the jamhub built-in effects won’t work on that microphone.… Weird, esoteric, I know. If you had a JamHub, you’d understand the quirk.

Anyhow, this RDL product solves my dilemma. It’s not perfect but it’s small (mounted with one strip of 3M Dual Lock) and it’s The only compressor I know of to both accept microphone level XLR and output microphone level XLR, compressed and limited.

I’d give it four stars but because it empowers me to do what I want, and nobody’s complained about it, we’ll call it an Amazon-5-star.

I purchased mine elsewhere.

title: Disappointing. Close but not worth it.
text:
I bought these so I could exercise without bringing my phone. I returned these after a few weeks mainly because:
1) Music organization is awful. Music playback occurs in alphabetical order based on the MP3's file name. The order doesn't pick back up where it left off either, and there is **no shuffle function**. If you copy 200 songs to the earbuds and you want to build a playlist of "workout songs", you have to use the phone app (not the PC app) and scroll through tons of MP3 file names and pick the ones you want. If you have a thousand songs copied, this is a real problem. Remember, you're not seeing a list of tracks broken up by artist, you're seeing...
"1 - Track by artist A.mp3"
"1 - Track by artist B.mp3"
"1 - Track by artist C.mp3"
"2 - Track by artist A.mp3"
and so on. Looking to listen to a new album you recently got? I hope you're OK with scrolling through a hundred other tracks and finding the ones you want based on their filename. It seems like using these as standalone music players was an afterthought and is not well designed at all.
Again, no shuffle functionality. This was a big deal breaker. I only ever heard the first 10 songs in my library, and adding songs to the two built-in playlists is archaic (no support for custom playlists). I have no idea why they'd overlook one of the basic features of all MP3 players in place since the mid 90's.
2) Ambient sound doesn't work well in windy environments. This includes while running or walking in an environment with even light wind. The microphones pick up wind very easily. Just as easily as talking on the phone in a windy environment does. I ended up turning ambient sound off a lot, but then I couldn't hear cars around me, etc. By the way, to turn ambient sound on and off you hold your finger on the touch sensor as it cycles through options verbally, then you let go to select that option. Ambient sound is option 3 (2 if your phone isn't connected) and it takes a few seconds to get to. I really wish you could reorder the options because option 1, "voice command", doesn't work that well and option 2, "begin workout with pace setter", is not useful to me. To turn ambient sound on/off, you have to hold the sensor for like 6 seconds. They couldn't figure out a better way to utilize that awesome touch sensor?
3) The sound of my face and neck muscles was consistently very apparent and annoying. Plug your ears and smile. This is what you'll hear all the time with these in. Every step you take is booming, especially while running.

I had one issue where only one of the buds was playing music. I left for the gym and the whole time I was there, only one was playing music, despite being able to control music with the other (silent) earbud. I got home and put them back in the charging case, and the problem stopped. I wish there was a power button on these things (or hey, use that touch sensor as a power button too). I've also heard them get out of sync slightly during a call, so one ear will hear the person's voice a little before the other ear and it's very distracting, almost like an echo.

Other than that, these are comfortable enough to wear for a while (about 1.5hrs at most for me). They don't fall out easily at all (even while shaking your head pretty roughly). Battery life is okay but not great. They look stylish. The touch sensor works well enough. I really wanted to like these earbuds. I suspect that just as with the first few Samsung smartwatches, it will probably take a few revisions to iron out the kinks. I didn't like my Gear S2 but my Gear S3 is a solid watch. I hope the technology improves because if they fix these issues, I would be very interested in buying the next revision in the future. They're close, but these problems are too big to ignore (for me at least), especially for the price point they sell for.

title: Good radios, but they come with a serious and potentially costly caveat
text:
While slightly more expensive than some other similar 16 channel consumer radios like the BaoFeng BF-888S, I feel the slenderness and knob design give these better ergonomics than the others. I’ve purchased two four packs of these, and have had no issues with them, and I’m able to use them in conjunction with other similar consumer UHF radios, dual band ham radios, and commercial UHF radios (as seen in the third photo). They’re easily programmable with a free program called Chirp and a ~$20 - $25 programming cable such as the Kenwood KPG-22 or BaoFeng PC03 (shown in fourth photo).
With the 400 - 470 MHz band split, they’re capable of being programmed with LMR, 70 centimeter ham, and FRS/GMRS frequencies, and are capable of being programmed for dual simplex and half duplex operation (and you can even make an impromptu repeater out of them with a Surecom duplex controller). While these have no FCC type acceptance I’m aware of and would only actually be legal for ham use, I can’t really condemn their use for FRS for the simple reason that FRS radios are often used as kids toys. These can be programmed to use non-standard DCS tones (so-called “privacy tones”) which won’t be found on the menus of these little blister pack FRS radios. So, if Chester the Child Molester is running around and scanning FRS frequencies with a blister pack radio, the one he’s using won’t be able to be programmed to the non-standard DCS tones, and be won’t be able to talk to your kids. Now, if Chester is a bit more advanced in radio, that’ll be a different matter.
Also, you have the ability to limit the number of channels available, so if you as a parent keep one on hand to monitor your kids, it’s a bit easier than trying to sift through 22 channels and 121 tones (2684 possible combination if you include carrier Squelch without the use of tones).
Now, where you need to be forewarned - whoever is answering questions here on Amazon on behalf of the seller/manufacturer has shown to be lacking in their knowledge of FCC law and band/frequency allocations in the US. In the second photo, I’ve downloaded the frequencies and settings from a radio just taken out of the box into the Chirp program. Aside from channels 6 and 7 (which are FRS/GMRS 18 and FRS/GMRS 22, respectively), all of the frequencies it comes programmed with are LMR (Land Mobile Radio) frequencies in the US, which may be allocated to private businesses or to public services in the US. If you key these up out of the box and interfere with the communications of a licensed private business or especially any public service/public safety organization, you seriously risk getting your feet held to the fire by the FCC. And the FCC like a particular number when they levy fines - 10,000. So yes, in spite of what the seller or these yahoos on here who know absolutely zero about radio may tell you, that is a big deal and is potentially very disastrous. So, you shouldn’t buy these unless you’re willing to spend an additional $20 - $25 for a programming cable such as the Kenwood KPG-22 or BaoFeng PC03 and the time to learn how to use Chirp (a free program that works for programming a vast majority of these Chinese import consumer radios). Or, if you get the programming cable and download Chirp, contact me and I’ll put together a Chirp image file for you that’ll keep you out of hot water and even provide you with a tutorial on how to use it if need be.

title: Generic
text:
Since the Mirrorless Interchangeable Lens Camera (MILC) revolution began, I’ve read several books on such cameras, as well as invested a substantial amount of money in equipment. These books were for the most part aimed at specific camera bodies and technical, telling you which button to press for which menu item and what the effect of pressing the button would be. This is the first book I’ve encountered dealing generically with the field of MILCs. Unfortunately most of the advice is also generic, applicable to DSLRs, rangefinders, twin lens reflexes and perhaps even view cameras.

The lead chapter deals with a description of what makes an MILC an MILC. The same chapter lists the advantages and disadvantages of MILCs compared to DSLRs. Anchell opines that the MILC is better in every category with a vengeance that almost rises to vendetta. He totally ignores such DSLR features as live view. Ultimately, the difference is that the electronic viewfinder can show you exactly what the final image will look like, and that MILCs are lighter. Even though I suspect that in the next few years MILCs may satisfy all my photography needs, at the present time, I still use my DSLR for several genres.

The chapters dealing with exposure, focus, lens selection and other subjects could just as well have been written about other body types. In a few cases, like his discussion of the three-legged stool approach to exposure, I found that, compared to other writers, he lacked clarity.

When I got to the chapter by guest writers, each dealing with their own genres (like weddings or wildlife) most of the discussions were just as applicable to DSLRs. The chapter on MILC controls dealt mostly with the Sony cameras that the author used, although where applicable there was brief reference to similar controls in other camera makes.

The chapter on post processing gave the author a chance to offer a few of his opinions about software. Like most photographers, he is a fan of keywords, although I was not certain he realizes how they made file structures far less important. I found his snide remarks about Adobe positively offensive.

When I got to the chapter on video, I was surprised that Anchell’s reason to learn video was for the commercial photographer to respond to client requests. There was little recognition that video might be a way to help the photographer better able to realize his vision in some situations. I chuckled when a heading in this chapter was “Tips for making a successful DSLR video.”

Just who is this book meant for? An experienced photographer will be able to find the benefits of MILCs with just a few seconds on line. A beginner might learn something about photography, although he or she probably will learn more useful information from a book aimed at his specific camera body. However, if you’re a tyro, given the rapid proliferation of MILCs, there may not be a book aimed at your specific camera body yet. Then this might provide an interim fix.

Note: The publisher provided me with a review copy of this book at no charge.

title: Best replacement for a Samsung Note 10+
text:
I got my Edge when it was on sale for $400 a week ago. My $1100 Samsung Note 10+ failed on me after just 1 year so I needed a replacement. I refuse to buy anymore Samsung devices because they aren't reliable. They are extremely expensive and short-lived. So it became time to switch brands and I chose Motorola.

So far I'm loving my Edge. The battery life is excellent. The overall speed of the system is easily as fast as the Note 10. The fingerprint sensor is way faster than ANY Samsung phone. And even face unlock is faster. The only downside so far are system updates. Currently my Edge has October security patch, and that was receive just a couple days ago (Nov. 15, 2020). But Motorola has promised to update it to Android 11 at some point this year.

The 5G networking on T-Mobile is producing a much better data signal than my 4G Note 10+. In fact, at home in Oklahoma City...around some high quality and numerous cell towers (according to T-Mobile customer service) I couldn't any signal at all with my Note 10+. But my Edge is providing on average around 50Mb/s. Sometimes it will measure over 100Mb/s, sometimes below 30Mb/s.

I've read about the Edge having "screen issues" and I'm keeping an eye out for them, but so far the display is gorgeous. Everything about this phone is satisfying...with the exception of finding a high-quality, name brand case for it. There are none other than overly-expensive Otterbox. No Spigen, no Caseology etc.

I did find a case from Dzxouui that is working well, but I had to make a gasket (from some shelving material made of 1mm or 2mm thick rubber and held it in place on the phone with some Glue Stick) for the camera hole on the back because it has a significant gap between the hole and the back of the phone that allows dust and particulates to enter easily.

Words of advice: Avoid Samsung phones.

text:

Early drivers struggled to hand normal tasks like web browsing and multi-monitor support. Gaming stability has been a nightmare, with the first round of drivers i used (19.7.2) crashing out of almost half of all games I tried to play. Newer driver have seemed to improved stability, but not by enough. I cannot get many popular titles to work at all even with the latest drivers installed on a clean windows 10 install.

With the 19.8.1 drivers I still have the following issues.

-All Ubisoft titles I own (Assassins Creed Odyssey, Far Cry (3,4,Primal)) will load into the game menu but then crash when I try to load an actual game.

- Witcher 3 loads into the game menu and crashes when the game attempts to load.

-Hellblade Senua's Sacrifice crashes before the menu can even appear

-Bioshock Infinite loads into the game but crashes after a few minutes of gameplay.

These are just the problems I've encountered from my very limited testing. I do not know if the issues are hardware or driver related, but they appear to be primarily driver issues. I ran Unigine Heaven benchmark and it runs fine in opengl and directx 9 modes, but immediately crashes in directx 11 mode. It seems most of the crashes occur when running modern, graphically intensive 3D titles that use the more recent directx versions.

All of these issues have been time consuming and exhausting to troubleshoot, and it is made even worse by the fact that there is still no solution. I have spent many hours installing and uninstalling drivers, reinstalling windows, and updating all the drivers and bios on my system. At this point all I want is something that works.

I paid an extra $3 to get the silver over the black because I thought it would have more metal, which it does. The silver is an aluminum top to the drive. The black is plastic, which is not only flimsier but also makes the drive run hotter. Aluminum conducts heat well. I don't understand why they don't make all of these things completely out of aluminum...

I was expecting to have to format the drive, but it was working immediately on my MacBook Pro, and almost immediately on my PC desktop (took a minute to auto-install drivers). Without formatting, I could use on the Mac and PC. I did not install any of the Seagate software.

I measured the actual write speeds for both PC and Mac, and they are both averaging 80-100 MB/sec. That was way faster than my old 1 TB drive, so I was pleasantly surprised with this drive.

I have only used this 1 day, so I will update if there are any issues in the next couple years.

title: Not what I had expected
text:
This review is a bit late, but better late than never.

I generally prefer analog or basic digital watches, but I got nibbled on by the smartwatch bug and figured I would try one out. I did not want to spend a ton of money on something, so I found this one and it seemed like a good deal for the price (it was already an older model, was refurbished, etc.). At the time, I was using this with a Samsung S4 phone and this watch was a nightmare to set up. First off, the watch did not come with the latest updates and they were extremely difficult to get installed (a known problem once I started digging into it). Once I got it updated, it would not remain synchronized with my phone consistently enough to make it worth my while to have a smartwatch (and I am NOT a heavy phone user, not even in the least).

Battery - battery life was a joke. Even keeping the watch on the lowest settings possible (and bearing in mind that I rarely use my phone), I was lucky if I got 24 hours of battery life. This was also a known problem and, to be fair, I suppose it's a fairly common problem with smart watches in the first place (by comparison, my phone would go 4 days before I needed to charge it).

Notifications drove me nuts - there is NO audible notification for incoming call, text, etc., just vibration alerts that were so mild I didn't even notice that it was vibrating 99% of the time. Why in the world is there no audible alert for receiving messages or calls?

About the only thing positive I have to say is that the watch seemed to be built solid enough and I liked the way it looked. I did like the fact that you could create your own custom watch faces via various programs, but the novelty wasn't enough to deal with the frustrations I had with it. I'm now back to a cheap Timex and I'll never waste money on a smart watch again.

title: Great value with good power handling and sound for a shallow mount coax
text:
I haven't always been impressed with Kicker products over the years but I think these are a solid value. I used to compete in and judge IASCA competitions in the mid 90s (I'm old) so I'm pretty particular about my speakers, especially the characteristics of the high range drivers. I don't go all out like in those days but I still appreciate good sound. These are going in the kick panels in my 73 project truck. I appreciate that they have good power handling and excursion specs but still maintain a shallow mounting depth. These things are important, as my mounting options were pretty limited in the factory locations and I plan to feed them 100watts RMS CEA rated and really give them the knob at times.

I listened to a lot of things locally, and for the price these really stood out. The high end had a brightness and clarity without being too sharp or sibilant, and they had good off-axis dispersion. I think they will cut through road noise without being harsh. The main drivers had a warmth and presence I preferred, with good midbass extention for their size but without compromising midrange clarity. There were 1 or 2 other good options in this price range but this was the most balanced package and the most appealing to my ear.

The covers are a bit flashy for my tastes and offer less protection than I'd like to see in a kick panel so I will use other covers but I can appreciate the design element.

title: very powerful - will secure your network
text:
I selected the 3100 after considering a number of competing products from Cisco, Ubiquity, Fortnet, etc. for a SOHO small office home office application. I like the open source pfsense as opposed to proprietary software. Open source is more secure and does not have back doors and is otherwise vetted. Note that Ubiquity firewall has a phone home feature that was not announced to users and cannot be turned off. The Netgate 3100 undergoes final assembly in Texas, which I appreciate particularly from a security standpoint.
After speaking with the sales rep at Netgate, I selected the 3100 instead of the 1100 because the 3100 is more powerful machine that can accommodate gigabit internet (which I do not presently have). The 1100 would probably be sufficient.
You do have to have some minimal technical ability to use this - basic familiarity with computers, networks, etc but you do not need to be a total nerd. Initial set up was pretty easy. Pro tips: 1) turn off your vpn, antivirus, etc. 2)reboot your cable modem after connecting the box.The rest is pretty straight forward.
After initial set up, the 3100 needs to be configured, packages uploaded, and so forth. I followed the YouTube videos from Lawrence Systems that are very detailed and well done. Kudos to them. Netgate also has instructional videos but I have not explored these in any great detail. Feel like I have secured my network.

Currently running Snort and pfBlocker among other packages. Very easy install and does not tax this machine at all.

Be cautioned that this device is not plug it in and forget it. It does take some time and effort to work through configurations in order to get the most out of this device. Really a whole world if one were to delve into it in a sophisticated fashion. Again, depending upon one's skills, a consultant such as a Netgate engineer may be needed to set this up particularly in more complex use cases.

Learn to use the terminal interface. I managed to brick this a couple of times playing with it during set up and revived it by using the USB connector and accessing it using the terminal on my mac.

FYI I use a Zyxel wireless access point. Both the Netgate 3100 and the Zyxel AP are connected to an Eaton backup power supply that, in turn, is connected to a SurgeX surge protector. You should have a backup power supply as you don't just unplug this (or just unplug the Zyxel AP).

All in all the 3100 is a sophisticated machine that will handle small to medium sized offices and equivalent. An industrial/commercial class device - not some consumer grade junk. Has all sorts of capabilities for more sophisticated users and more complex use cases. Buy it. Take your time and set it up correctly and completely.

I have been using this for a couple of months now and have had no issues.

NC was good, not as good as sony - call quality was better than sony though. sound was also better - more impactful, much better soundstage, no sibilance detected - but the comfort killed me - returned them

Went to BB to check out the px7 - right next to them was the momentum3. They werent even on my radar, because i had the first pair of wired momentums years back, and they were too small for my huge ears. I figure though, since im there, might as well compare the two. Immediately i noticed that the sennheiser was quicker, explosive almost. It was a little bass heavy, but its customizable in the app - px7 was also bass heavy, but it felt more bloated and its not customizable. Music seperation was better, soundstage larger, mids a little pushed, but still sounded good. Sounc quality the momentums had it. Comfort was also best of the bunch. Lambskin really is delightful. It is hot, but its so comfy. NC is NOT anywhere near the other 3 I mentioned, but it is serviceable on a train, just turned up the volume a little bit and was good. better than nothing for sure.

most of the issues people talked about before have been resolved with updates to the firmware of the device and of the app, BT issues, static issues with MBP, turning it on and off while keeping the headphones open. All fixed. This made me feel comfortable knowing that the team at Sennheiser is listening. Overall, I recommend these over anything else.

title: Great sports headphones for runners
text:
I don't write too many reviews. But there's something I want to say with this pair of headphones. I've been using them for a few weeks. For sure I can't vouch for its durability. But I'd like to share my experience so far. For reasons I don't really know, most the US-based reviews came from Vine Voice reviewers - According to Amazon, they are a group of frequent reviewers who received the product for free in exchange for an honest review. That's very nice. But it's still a bit weird that almost all the reviews of the product were from the Vine Voice program members. I bought the headphones with my own money on Amazon. I might not be a regular reviewer, but in this case I have skin in the game.

Let me get this right off the bat. This is a great pair of sports headphones. The operative word is sports. Adidas is Adidas; it is not Sennheiser or other major headphone manufacturers. Adidas is a sports equipment company. I think when you consider buying this pair of headphones or earbuds, it might be wise to think of it as a sports accessory or equipment. I run almost everyday. I sweat profusely - the headphones have been holding up well and its IPX4 rating looks conservative. They are well-built and appear to be effectively sweat-proof. Battery life is excellent. For someone who spends about 8-9 hours on outdoor running each week, I just need to charge them once a week. The neckband is a great design. It has good weight - not too heavy, not too light. It is comfortable to wear. It doesn't dangle and it doesn't jump. It is unobtrusive. I love physical buttons. The three buttons on the right side of the neckband are easy to use, though it takes some getting used to to figure out the layout of the volume up and down buttons. The customizable button on the left side of the neckband is a neat feature. If you have Spotify, you can play your own playlist through your running watch (e.g., a Garmin Forerunner 645 Music) or your phone. I am not fast and I need every help I can get in that last mile of my run.

From reading other reviews, the biggest complaint about the headphones is the sound quality, or the lack thereof. I agree that they are not the best-sounding headphones. I have a limited vocabulary to describe sound quality. The sound is a bit grainy. It is a bit veiled. But honestly I think they only sound not as good in comparison. When I run, the sound produced by the headphones is clear and it is good-sounding enough. Bass is solid but not spectacular. You can also tweak the sound profile with the Adidas headphone app, which is basically an equalizer app. I don't know - bluetooth headphones have come a long way, but they are still not as good as wired headphones in the same or even cheaper price ranges. Bluetooth is compressed audio - you trade audio fidelity for convenience. I know there are more advanced codecs like aptX and aptX HD out there (BTW, I don't think these headphones support aptX) but when you're streaming from your sports watch or phone, the sound quality you get is only as good as the weakest link. So when you try to listen to 24-bit TIDAL MQA files on these headphones in a workout setting, or any bluetooth headphones for that matter, you'll lose some sound quality.

But the question is: can you discern what is in theory lost? YMMV I'm unfazed by its less than perfect sound. I ask myself how much I hear when I'm running hard (and I suppose you're only reading this review if you're interested in purchasing a pair of headphones for workouts). I hate to admit it but I have a hard time discerning CD quality sound from 320Kbps sound on Spotify when I sit still, let alone when my heart is beating at 180 bpm and my own pulse is thundering in my ears. As a pair of workout headphones, the sound quality is good enough. I give the Adidas sports headphones five stars - for its build quality and for its stable and unobtrusive design that leaves running unencumbered. I think it's no coincidence that the one Vine Voice reviewer who took the headphones for his runs (the person uploaded some pics) also gave them five stars.

title: Quality typing experience, solid body, but horrible keycaps and backlight. A+ support though.
text:
I purchased this keyboard directly from Azio about 4.5 months ago. My home office is retro/steampunk-themed, so the look of this keyboard was a perfect match. However, for $220, it’s simply not worth it. While the materials of the body are very solid and high quality, and the typing experience is pleasant, crisp and clicky, the keycaps and lighting are absolutely horrendous.

After only a few weeks of frequent use, the paint began to wear off around the letters. The keycaps are a clear ABS plastic that are painted everywhere except the letter leaving the clear letter exposed for the backlight to shine through. They don't add any kind of clear coat on top to even out the surface, so you can feel the indentation of each letter next to the surrounding paint, and if your nails catch the paint around the letters while typing, it will wear away the letter into a clear blob.

Azio's support team was great and sent out replacement caps around the 4-month mark for the keys that had worn out; however, in just a few short weeks they are once again wearing away (see S and N in photo). At this price point, I expected high-quality keycaps, not cheap clear ABS ones with sprayed on color. And, as this keyboard has custom switches, the caps cannot be swapped for higher-quality ones.

The second major issue for this keyboard is the lighting. The backlight is a white LED color with that classic unpleasant blue/purple undertone that we saw on the first generation of LED Christmas lights. It comes in 4 brightness levels: off, bright, very bright and blinding. So for anyone looking to have a subtle backlight, look elsewhere. In a dark room, even the lowest setting hurts my eyes to look at, so I keep it off which defeats the purpose of having a backlight to begin with.

Also, a couple weeks ago I started noticing that even when the backlight was off, some of the keys would still emit a very faint glow that would jump around the keyboard as I typed. I once again contacted Azio about this and they said it can happen when using a USB hub or if the cable is bad. As I don't use the former, I tried swapping cables, and computers and it still happened.

Support initially asked that I send the keyboard in for service, to which I explained as a software engineer who works from home, I'd have to purchase another keyboard while this was "in the shop" so I could continue to work. They agreed to do a one-time replacement where I signed a form and gave them a credit card to put a hold on. They are shipping a new keyboard and I just received FexEx confirmation. Once it arrives, I can send back my defective unit, and they will take the hold off my credit card. If they fail to receive the old one, they will process the charge for the new one. Seemed like a fair compromise, and I do commend them for having good support. They've been pleasant to work with; albeit, it sometimes takes a couple days for them to respond via email.

As my keyboard is always plugged in, I have not used the wireless features and cannot speak to them.

Once I receive my replacement, I plan to remove all the caps and spray them with a plastic-bonding satin clear coat to prevent the letters from chipping ($5 on Amazon). I also purchased glass paint, and I plan to put a dab of color on each of the LED backlights to decrease their brightness and harshness ($14 on Amazon). I'll update this when I do to let you know how it works out.

Bottom line:

Cost: 3/10 - This keyboard is simply priced too high for what it offers
Looks (new): 10/10 - Coolest-looking keyboard I've ever owned
Looks (used): 6/10 - Caps wear quickly and collect dust around their border
Feel: 9/10 - Typing is great but takes a little getting used to
Body Materials: 10/10 - Very solid and high-quality
Switches: 6/10 - Perfect travel and click, but don’t allow for custom caps
Keycaps: 2/10 - Great font & typewriter style, the rest is utter garbage
Lighting: 0/10 - Ugly blinding white light that is too bright to use in the dark
Wrist Rest: 6/10 - High quality, but the leather has pulled away from the foam, so it's lumpy after only a few months. I’d imagine the wood one lasts much longer.

If you want a retro/typewriter-style keyboard, this is probably your best bet at the moment. However, due to its shortcomings with the keycaps and lighting, I would only make the purchase again if it were in the $130ish range (because I do love the look), at which point I'd give it 3-4 stars. If Azio had PBT caps, died the plastic instead of painted it, or at least added a layer or coating on top of the current caps to prevent chipping and had better lighting options, it might be worth the price they are charging and I would probably give it a 5-star rating.

If you aren't jonesing for the retro look, there are much, much better options at this price point that will last a lot longer.

UPDATE (10-22-2019)

Bumping my review from 2 stars to 4.

I received the replacement keyboard, and while it didn’t have the lighting issue, the leather was scratched and scuffed up. You might think that should lower the rating, but I contacted support via email with photos and immediately received a call from Paul, who has been great to work with.

He agreed that the condition is unacceptable and apologized profusely. He offered to send another keyboard out, this time the Elwood as I expressed concerns over the leather quality in the most recent Gunmetal. At no charge to me, they will ship back both my original and the scuffed replacement and send a new Elwood along with an extra complete set of key caps. Paul said they are working with the manufacturer to try to improve the caps so they do not wear, and they are always incorporating customer feedback.

While I still think $220 is too high for the longevity of the keyboards, it looks like they are constantly trying to improve their products and listen to their customers. I’m very impressed with Azio support.

Also, I tested a dab of burnt sienna glass paint on one of the LEDs. I wiped it off shortly after as I’ll be returning they keyboard, but it transformed the ultra bright white into a subtle reddish-orange that looked great. I’ll be doing this to all my keys on the replacement and will upload photos.

As far as the clear coat spray paint - it’s a no-go. Once it dries it just peels off the cap as it does not bond to the paint they use. So I’m looking into other options to preserve the legends. I’ll update if I figure something out.

title: A great vehicle system and a great value!
text:
I'm really impressed with the A6 that Atoto designed and manufactures. I initially was just looking for a stereo replacement for my truck that would inexpensively play digital music and display a backup camera view. For about $50 Amazon offers a couple of versions under lots of company names. For another $50 you can find Android-based vehicle units. But the more I looked and compared, I kept coming back to the Atoto A6. In my opinion nothing else compares favorably.

Here my top ten reasons why I chose to spend a little more and go with the A6:
1. Bluetooth phone interface – not built into my vehicle so a must for me.
2. GPS – a vehicle-based GPS offered a larger screen and doesn't tie up my smart phone or deplete it's battery.
3. 1024 x 600 high brightness touchscreen
4. 3 USB interfaces and 1 micro SD. Lots of options for digital music and vehicle interfaces like the ODBII torque app or a TPS system.
5. Dual Bluetooth – phone interface on one, ODBII monitor, etc on 2nd BT
6. It offers 3 separate video inputs. I have a little fiberglass camper and also needed to occasionally view it's rear-facing camera. The A6 is already setup to automatically switch to a rear-facing camera and also is setup to record a front-facing (dash) camera.
7. Full Android tablet capabilities – any google play apps - google maps, waze, torque, etc!
8. AM/FM, sub-woofer output, 9 band EQ – many of the others don't offer all 3
9. The external WiFi antenna – not a big deal, but it just shows that Atoto is thinking ahead of most of the others. Allows the A6 to directly use WiFi anywhere your smart phone could. With a hotspot on your phone allows full connectivity.
10. Periodic OS updates provided by Atoto – another professional touch...

title: Check the voltage before using!
text:
I have ordered a bunch of these for a project. (20 total supplies) Of the ones I ordered, 2 of them were passing ~12v instead of the 5v or 3.3v. I also had two of them where the voltage jumpers were not connected right because the pins were bent, so the output for that side was zero volts. After straightening the pins, they were fine. In terms of voltage, they were generally within a 10th of a volt of the expected value, generally on the lower side. So, 4.93v instead of 5v or 3.22v instead of 3.3v. Also note that the power regulators run very hot ... like 2-3 seconds touch before it becomes uncomfortable. (I don't have another way of measuring it.) For my application, I replaced the pins that press into the prototyping breadboard with screw terminals, but I did check a few against a proto board and and it was a tight fit. In some cases, I needed to straighten the pins to get them to fit. I have left one of these running for 48 hours with a load and it worked fine for the entire period.

Given the price, to me, this are worth the money. Just make sure you test the voltage before putting it to any circuit.

text: I love the fact that with simply an HDMI cable, and a combined keyboard/trackpad(or ball), I can take this thing anywhere, even a hotel, and I have a full PC to watch whatever I want to. I have yet to see a hiccup in this thing after two months of constant use. My husband uses it as the household TV he enjoys, and he does not like complicated equipment. its simple to setup, just plug the hdmi cable into the back of your TV, plug in it's power supply,  and you have your pc going. it even had a harness for attaching it to the back of your tv. I bought a real monitor for it, but you dont have to. It is full-featured, has windows 10, and I can have at least a dozen tabs open at once, one of which is playing youtube, and another that is always open to email, along with whatever others. no lag, no skipping/buffering of the video. I would NOT say this thing is capable of running minecraft, nor is it good for Adobe art programs. not enough oomph. but for the average daily user it is great. It would be a perfect purchase for someone who travels a lot and doesnt want the bulk and risk of carrying around a laptop. this thing is about 5'' square, and will fit in  a tiny space. Also you cant really tell its a computer without looking close. it looks like a plastic box, so less likely to get stolen. The biggest downside I can see is the memory that comes with it. there isnt enough for someone that likes to save photo, video, and other programs. After I cleaned out all the bloatware I could out of windows 10, i had about 35GB leftover empty. MORE than enough for this pc's use as the house TV, but if you want to put any sort of programs on it, or use it as a photobook, or even just have a lot of files for your business, then I would recommend getting an external SSD drive for this. You can get TF cards as well. it has a slot for them, and you can also open it up and install newer, faster memory if you wish. Though it is fanless, the drive is solid state, so there are no moving parts to create friction heat. it DOES get warmish around the end of the day, when it's been on for 10-12 hours, but it does not overheat, and a small fan will chill it if you are worried about sensitive files.

title: Tips on how to improve rigidity
text:
As others have mentioned these will not hold your speakers immobile like cinderblocks or $200-$400 stands. The problem is that the steel base material is too thin and flexes when you apply sideways pressure on the uprights. This is more noticeable with heavy speakers and it is hard to say whether it affects performance in an audible way. If you're concerned you might epoxy an 8" to 9" round ceramic or cast iron trivet to the underside of the bottom plate to prevent it from flexing. A pair of these would probably do the trick: https://www.amazon.com/Lodge-L8DOT3-Trivet-Pre-Seasoned-8-inch/dp/B00063RXKQ

I salvaged a 3/8" thick pizza stone we were about to discard, cut 7-3/4" x 7-3/4" pieces using the glass cutter/wire hanger technique, and epoxied them to the underside of the base using several wood blocks and clamps. This worked better than I had hoped, and the stands are now very rigid! As a bonus the added weight makes them a little more stable as well.

Apart from that, kudos to the manufacturer for the functional yet attractive design, easy assembly, and for including carpet-piercing/leveling spikes, pads to protect hardwood floors, and spikes to level the speakers. Great value.

title: Converter works for my 48V to 12V led Light Bar Install and hope it will last
text: I purchased this transformer/converter along with a wiring harness to install a 20watt 12V LED light bar I had purchased a while back on Amazon and finally got around to installing it. I deducted 1 star because I wish the wire leads on the converter were about double the length to make the install a lot easier.  This review is not so much to just review the transformer, but the whole process in hopes it will help someone else figure out what to do and to know what to expect in a similar situation. In all it took me about 1 hour and 30 mins to do everything, but about 20 minutes of that was trying to figure out the best way to wire it and run the wires with the smallest footprint and more importantly easiest way to do it.  First, I mounted my light on the top of my cart roof as there were already two holes from the factory that looked like the perfect spot to install the bar. (Note regarding mounting the light here: In hindsight it looks good, but the light projection shows every bounce my cart hits because the roof isn't very rigid and moves a good bit with every bump I hit and probably would have been better if I mounted it to the cart itself on a more rigid base that didn't jiggle as much.) Anyhow back to the wiring of it.  I deducted 1 star for two reasons.  The length of the wiring harness is a bit short and the wire terminals wouldn't hold.  The wire length was part of my issue with trying to figure out the best way to run the wires and making sure everything was connected without having to go to the store and buy more wire to extend everything.  I finally had a game plan and just did have enough wire to reach everywhere and wanted to share in case there are others looking to add a light to their Golf cart without having to buy extra wire too.  My cart is an 48V electric Yamaha Golf Cart by the way.  I also purchased a 48V to 12V transformer so that I could run the light off the whole battery pack and not just a couple batteries to get an accurate 12V and because that way it would draw from all batteries equally.  With regards to the transformer I didn't want to secure the transformer on top of the batteries because sometimes transformers fail and can short out and burn up so I found a spot on the frame behind the battery pack bay to mount it and also allow for more air to circulate around it and hopefully allow it more cooling when using it so that it will last.  To connect the wire harness to the transformer and then the battery pack I cut the battery terminals off and spliced in the transformer using WAGO nut connectors (these are my favorite type of wire connectors)  I mounted the relay close to the batter pack also on one of the upright frames in the battery pack bay.  Due to the short length of the toggle switch I couldn't run the switch to the front dash near the key so I had to mount the switch just under the seat where I could easily reach down and turn it on when needed.  I did have to drill a couple holes in my cart, but put them where it was difficult to see and where the footprint would be as small as possible.  As for the wire that went to the light I found an opening underneath the battery pack bay and pulled the wire through there and under the cart zip tying the cable secure along the way.  I ran the wire up to the passenger side front wheel well then drilled a hole inside the passenger side accessory compartment and them up the front support rail then up to the roof where I connected it to the light.  This wiring harness has two connections for two lights, but I only used the one and tied off the other underneath the wheel well.  Overall the price for what I bought is good, but if the wiring harness was about 50% longer on the wire to the light and for the red toggle switch it would be able to have more options for installing.  I am happy however, and after I completed my project the light works great. I did change the 15AMP fuse to the 10AMP fuse since my light is rated for 10AMP.  The wiring harness I purchased for about $10 also comes with a few extra wire terminals and three extra fuses (2 extra 15amp and one 10amp).  I don't recommend the wire terminal connectors because I couldn't get them to hold and decide to cut them off and just wire the light direct and tape them up with electrical tape instead where it connected to my LED light lead.  Anyhow hope this helps someone figure out how to install and LED light to an electric golf cart.  If the converter fails I will update my review.  I don't plan to use my light bar a lot, but do hope the converter lasts more than a year for the price as that is the only item that I can imagine having an issue with if I every had one.  I would post pictures of my install, but there isn't a link to add pictures to this review.  Not sure what is going on with regards to not being able to attach pictures as the saying goes a picture is worth 1,000 words and by the time you finish reading this I'm sure you would have like to see some pictures.

title: These ARE balanced, despite some of the reviews
text:
Several of the reviews here state these are not balanced, on the grounds that they only had 3 cables running from the plug to the earbuds, and thus they must be sharing/shorting one of the pins.

A few seconds with a multimeter shows that none of the pins are shorted, and that there are clearly 2 distinct pair of wires running to the earbuds - presumably with one of the physical cables having 2 separate internal cables.

From a sound quality perspective these are an excellent headphone for the price. I own both the balanced (2.5mm plug) and unbalanced (3.5mm plug) versions and realistically I don't think I can tell the difference between the two when connected to an Ear Studio ES-100 DAC, but they both provide clean, natural sound with reasonable isolation, a great soundstage for earbuds, and are extremely comfortable to wear even for long periods of time.

title: New speakers changed my listening life!
text:
I'd been debating upgrading my terrible sounding home stereo but I'd find myself thinking I don't listen to enough music, and then I thought, hey wait a minute....

So I did some research. Lots. Ended up getting a pair of Q Acoustics 3020i Bookshelf speakers.

The difference between these and my old Boston Acoustics was amazing! The old ones had a kind of harsh, muddy sound - just awful.
The Q Acoustics are smooth and easy to listen to and very clear - in fact I heard stuff on these I had never heard before on records Id been listening to for 20, 30, 40 years. (Even using Spotify!) There is a hard to describe 3 dimensional quality to the sound from these. Pretty broad response high to low, seemingly without any hyped frequencies. In my set-up I've got a little subwoofer that gives it a little extra oomph. I just use a touch of it. (I wish the live sound mixing guys would use just a tad.)
I listened to:
Lucinda Williams - Car Wheels on a Gravel Road
Tom Petty - Wildflowers
Pat Metheny - Are You Going With Me?
Bill Frisell - Surfer Gurl
Pink Floyd - Breathe
Donald Fagen - New Frontier (classic track live sound guys often use to tune a room)
Shawn Colvin - A Few Small Repairs

The drums sound amazing. I hear the stick hit the low tom and the sound of the drum room. Guitars sound incredible as well. Acoustics feel like you're sitting right in front of them. A Tele on the Lucinda track sounds like my Deluxe Reverb is in the room.
Vocals are fantastic - full and clear but not strident. Little parts like mandolins, background guitar parts, Wurlitzer, and subtle B3 notes are so present - still low in the mix but way more easy to hear. Nice musical bass - full but not boomy or thumpy. The stereo image is really great. The speakers seem to really shine on some pleasing frequencies that get left out of a lot of current systems found in cars or Bluetooth portables, ear buds, Google and Amazon virtual assistants.

I should've done this a long time ago. It's super inspiring to listen to music on these speakers.

text: I have  owned this binocular and the Swaro Mountain CL 8X25 at the same time and also have the Zeiss Terra 10x32 and the Zeiss Conquest 8x32 along with other alpha binoculars. People here are  getting carried away and just kidding themselves. They are a bit better on sharpness and color rendition than my Zeiss Terra 10x32s but not by that much. They are a very decent 8x25 binocular for the money I agree and the best in that price range, but people are over rating them here by comparison. Their color rendition, clarity and definition to the edge are no match for the Swaro Mountains. I gave my Zeiss 8x25s  away to a friend, who needed them for a long trip to distant parts, but will replace them in time as I collect good binoculars and review them. These are an excellent buy for the price and reasonably well made. But so are my Zeiss Terra 10x32s, however.

title: SSK 1000Mpbs NVME SSD Ultra Speed External SSD
text:
This was a gift from my mother, so I thought I would give it a run to see how it will do before I take it on our trip. My plan was to use the SSK SSD drive with my Samsung Note 9 to allow me to backup pictures where WiFi and Cellular service will not be available. I was curious about how this drive would perform, so I ran some tests (see below) and I gave this a 5 rating based on these results.

Here is how I ran my tests:

SETUP: File Size: 1000 Mbyte and 4000 Mbyte and Block Size: 1 Mbyte. The Software used is Parkdale V2.99. I tested this on two computers, a desktop PC and an a notebook PC. The desktop computer is an i7 Desktop with 32GB RAM and a USB 3.1 port. The Notebook is a Lenovo YOGA 700-11ISK 2 in 1 with USB Port 3.0 port (it does not have USB 3.1).

TESTS: Files size at 1000 Byte: Since I do not have anything like the SSK Portable SSD drive to compare to, I ran an initial test using the desktop PC’s SSD Drive. It uses a Samsung SSD 850 EVO for Drive C and it is connected to a SATA III Port:
>> Samsung SSD 850 EVO 500GB - EMT02B6Q 448.7 GB Local Disk (C:): 499.3 MByte/sec read, 475.4 MByte/sec write

>> That same test with File size at 4000 Mbytes
Samsung SSD 850 EVO 500GB - EMT02B6Q 448.7 GB Local Disk (C:): 493.8 MByte/sec read, 472.6 MByte/sec write

File size 1000 Mbyte: Now the SSK Portable NVME SSD Ultra Speed External Solid State Drive USB-C USB3.1 Gen 2 External SSD with 1000Mbps Data Transfer for Laptop, Tablet and Type C Phones (1TB) connected to the i7 Desktop’s USB 3.1 port:
>> SSK - 0206 953.8 GB Local Disk (J:): 402.4 MByte/sec read, 389.6 MByte/sec write USB

File size at 4000 Mbyte:
SSK - 0206 953.8 GB Local Disk (J:): 403.5 MByte/sec read, 392.2 MByte/sec write USB (not a significant difference).

USB CABLES: This device comes with two USB cables: a USB Type “A” to Type a micro “B” connector; and a Type “C” to Type “C” cable.

On the i7 Desktop PC, comparing the SSK portable SSD drive to my Drive C, the SSK Drive seems to perform quite well. As for connecting it to a phone with a USB Type C connector, that remains a test I will do later on the Note 9 as I have no other devices that uses the Type “C” connector.

DRIVE SPECS:
EVO SSD Drive Specs and Performance: Sequential Read: Max. 540 MB/s and Sequential Write: Max. 520 MB/s
M.2. NVME SSD: The SSK SSD box says it has an M.2. NVME SSD, so I found specs for this SSD online and the basic Read performance spec is up to 520MB/s and the Write Performance is up to 210MB/s.

TES ON THE NOTEBOOK:
Another test I did was to try the SSK Portable SSD drive on a notebook computer. For this test, I used my Lenovo YOGA 700-11ISK 2 in 1 with USB Port 3.0.

The SSK Portable SSD attached through the USB 3.0 port and the controller's write caching set to quick removal (no caching):
SSK - 0206 953.8 GB Local Disk (D:): 393.2 MByte/sec read, 379.2 MByte/sec write USB

COMPARED TO OTHER PORTABLE DRIVES:
Here is a test using a SanDisk 1.28GB Ultra Fit drive with the controller's write caching set tp quick removal (no caching)
SanDisk - Ultra Fit - 1.00 115.7 GB Data (E:): 132.6 MByte/sec read, 62.1 MByte/sec write USB

That same drive with the controller's write caching enabled
SanDisk - Ultra Fit - 1.00 115.7 GB Data (E:): 129.9 MByte/sec read, 62.3 MByte/sec write USB

The Lenovo’s Drive C. A Samsung SSD 860 EVO M.2 500GB drive:
Samsung SSD 860 EVO M.2 500GB - RVT21B6Q 401.0 GB Windows (C:): 1078.8 MByte/sec read, 299.9 MByte/sec write

Here is the test with an external Portable M.2 Kingshare controller, with a Samsung 128GB M.2. drive and the controller's write caching set to quick removal (no caching)
SAMSUNG - MZNLN128HCGR-000L2 - EMT23L0Q 101.0 GB Windows (F:): 362.1 MByte/sec read, 97.7 MByte/sec write USB

That same drive set with the controller's write caching enabled
SAMSUNG - MZNLN128HCGR-000L2 - EMT23L0Q 101.0 GB Windows (F:): 348.2 MByte/sec read, 117.0 MByte/sec write USB

CONCLUSION: Your test results and experience with the SSK SSD drive may differ depending on how you are using the drive and what device you will connecting it to, but considering the performance on the notebook, I am pleased with the drive’s performance, and I recommend it for anyone who needs a 1TB portable drive with some performance gains on a notebook/laptop/desktop PC over a portable mechanical or hybrid drive.

title: Macbook Air 2017 repaste. Drops my Idle from 60C to 46C, and load from 95C to 70C... Amazing
text: Got the 2019 MX4 2 Gram tube... The Review: As you can see, the factory didn't even  put thermal paste on the integrated GPU, and after only a single year the OEM CPU paste either evaporated or put practically nothing.  MX4 spreads amazing. Just put a ball bearing size amount on the GPU and 3 ball bearing on the CPU (might be too much, but it spreads so well anyway), the application was probably the easiest Ive ever done out of dozens of PCs and Macs Ive rebuilt over the last 20 years. MX4 is also slightly adhesive so it was easy to mount that tiny macbook heatsink. I used to be an Arctic Silver 5 and Ceramique 2 disciple, but I am converted to MX4. I am noticing a small curing period. I started at idle initially at 70C and got worried ( original was 60C) but after an hour its doing about 46C at idle CPU and fan speeds.  As a bonus, I can max out my Intel I5 5350u at 2.7Ghz while running at only 70C and a Fan speed of 4500RPM. Amazing 25C drop and 2000RPM fan drop! Previously it was 95C at 6500RPM with the OEM paste.  Also, I've noticed that my GPU has come to life! Because there was no thermal grease, it stuck to 350MHZ. Now it always wants to throttle up to 1GHz all the time! I wish I didn't wait a year and just replaced the thermal grease when I got it. One tip, be gentle on your screws in that macbook, the grommets for the screws are glued on. They pop off easily, watch that torque on those tiny T5 screws. Also, used only 25% of my 2G tube.  You will get at least 3 desktops or 4 laptop repastes out of this tube.
