title: Decent speaker, but the voice ....
text:
I got this speaker a week ago for Christmas and have used it almost every day since. This speaker is decent. It paired quickly with my phone and plays the audio as expected. I can control the volume from my phone. I really wanted a bluetooth speaker that also had an FM radio and this one fit the bill. The FM radio works fairly well. There is some static at times, but I just need to reposition the radio and that usually solves the problem.

Now for the negative. The power button and the mode changing button seem like they are not going to last. Sometimes I have to press multiple times before the button does it job. Sometimes the button gets stuck under the metal frame that surrounds it. The buttons just seem cheap. Also, you cannot choose the FM presets. An automatic function assigns every FM station to a number. But that's not a super big deal since you can just directly type in the digits of your FM station frequency to go directly to the station you want. But the worst negative by far is the half-intelligible voice with a strong Asian accent that tells you "Bluetooth mode - Pairing!" every single d*** time you turn the radio on. (I didn't know it was saying "pairing" until I saw that another reviewer had deciphered it -- it is not obvious due to the unclear pronunciation.) And each time you change the mode from Bluetooth to FM to Line-in mode, the half-intelligible Asian voice declares what mode you are in. Logically, I know that this shouldn't bother me so much. But it does! It's like nails on a chalkboard. And I am a language teacher with a high tolerance for variation in language usage. This isn't something I'm looking for in my devices.

I would give 4.5 stars if it were not for the voice. If I had the chance to buy this speaker again, I would instead go looking for a different one given the plethora of offerings on Amazon. I would definitely look for one that doesn't talk to me in heavily Asian-tinged English.

title: Almost perfect,  but....
text:
I bought this backpack in preparation for a trip to Japan and Korea and overall was happy with it after wearing it all day every day for nearly two weeks straight. Usually my wife carries a large bag around with us on vacation but I wanted to be prepared to be out all day in a changing climate so I picked this up for myself. Honestly for the price compared to other travel backpacks I researched this was well worth it.

Pros:
Storage space - I had more than enough room for everything I needed. This will be my new go to "personal item" for flights where I don't want to pack a suitcase or a carry-on.

Pockets - I found the auxiliary pockets to be conveniently placed and provided ample room to conveniently organize my sunglasses container, headphones, and all my other travel essentials.

Hidden zippers - I also liked that the two front pockets have zippers that are more hidden. Someone had tried to pick-pocket my wife in Rome a few years ago by going through her backpack on the street so I was happy to see these zippers are out of sight - making you less of a target.

RFID pocket - this was a major win for me! Carrying around passports, contactless credit cards and international driving license documents everywhere while traveling is scary. I've always been afraid of losing them or having them stolen. The secret pocket here sits right in the small of your back while wearing the pack and I found it to be accessible without having to take the pack off. Thanks to the location however I would certainly notice if someone was trying to steal them from me. This pocket is also covered in a padded material making the pack even more comfortable to carry! This padding also helps to hide the fact that it's a pocket so when taking off to set down I never worried about someone trying to go through it.

Padded laptop and sleeve - I dont travel with a laptop but I did throw my Nintendo Switch console in the laptop sleeve. It was protected during the flight and all over town. I can see how the way the laptop pocket opens would be convenient for traveling with a computer but it is not a feature that I need.

Comfort - I FILLED this most days while out and it got pretty heavy, especially during two open to close days at Disney, but I never experienced any back pain from carrying this. The padding over the RFID pocket helped here.

Style - I would take functionality over style any day bit this backpack offers the best of both worlds. I love the sleek look ot jas.

Cons:
My biggest disappointment with this backpack was the shoulder strap USB port. One of my main reasons for buying this was to be able to plug my portable charger into the backpack itself and then have the freedom to plug in my phone cable to the built in charging port on the shoulder strap. Unfortunately for me the USB port on mine is junk. It works, don't get me wrong but the components are such poor quality that my phone was not able to draw a charge from it. It would show that it was charging but if I used it while plugged in the battery would continue to go down. I ended up just running my charging cable through the headphone hole directly to my portable charger and then it would charge just fine. Still, when this was a major deciding factor in my purchase it left me disappointed.

Mesh side pockets - Okay, so these fit my 32 oz. Nalgene bottle which is what I was hoping to use them for. The only problem for me was that the pocket was not quite deep enough and the elastic was not quite tight enough to hold it in place. This meant whenever I laid my backpack down (overhead storage on the plain/train) my water bottle slipped out and would roll around. I ended up using a carabiner to attach the bottle to the main zipper on the backpack to keep it in place but with a regular plastic water bottle you wouldn't have that option.

Overall this backpack is great. I would recommend it and I would buy it again. I can't speak to strength and durability yet as I only used it for the one vacation so far but it held up just fine for me and I found workarounds for my only two issues.

title: Easy to install, up and running in 5-10 minutes
text:
I purchased this from Cyber_Geek was sent Priority Mail from NYC. This router/gateway was used to replace an Verizon Actiontec router that was working fine but is only an 2.4 GHz band wireless router.

This used router had very minor scuffs and a missing HAN cover from the back of the router. This does not effect the operation of the router but is a cosmetic flaw. It had a tag saying "Tested and Functional" on it. After releasing the Broadband/Coax IP address in the Actiontec (you need to log into the Actiontec to do this) I unplugged the power from the Actiontec so it would not renew the IP Address before I connected this Verizon G1100. I then connected the cables to the G1100 and powered it up. After 5-10 minutes, I was able to log into the G1100 from the connected PC without an issue. I was able to use the Verizon My FiOS app to log into the router remotely, which you can not do with the Actiontec router.

This used router is being used in a business location, not for home use. It is running digital phones and wireless building thermostats, cams, printer, PC, STB. I have used it for more than a week and there are NO issues with this router/gateway so far. I am getting more speed than what the Actiontec was getting, I measured 5-6 meg more. The wireless coverage is the same with this router. I have seen no improvement as it has to cover two buildings and the walls are quite thick. The 2.4 GHZ band is used more here because of the distance the signal has to travel.

I would make sure if you buy a used router and going to use it with Verizon service, you stick with Verizon firmware installed on the router already. I know how to overcome tech problems, but I would not advise starting with the wrong brand firmware to begin with. Also you will see all the old devices that the router was connected to in its past life. To remove them you need to assign a static ip to each one and THEN remove them. There is no easy way to remove them in the router GUI, but leaving them will cause no harm to the router operation anyway. Update: The new firmware that Verizon now has allows you to remove old devices much easily now. The router still works without a problem. Feb 2021

title: Simple design  and works well, but could be better
text:
I'm using this to be able to share a pair of speakers between 2 stereo amplifiers. It seems to work well. I don't hear any sound degradation.
However, before I used it I removed the cover. I've attached a photo. The first thing I noticed is they put a 100 ohm, 5 watt resister on each amp input. This is to keep a load on the amp, even when it's deselected. This isn't usually critical on solid state amps, but is for tube amps. When switched on, the much larger 100 ohms should have no noticeable effect on a 4 or 8 ohm load from the speakers.
The second thing I noticed is the leads on the 100 ohm resisters weren't insulated. On my device, one lead in particular was maybe 2-3mm away from touching the case. A little too close for me. To be safe I put some electrical tape over all of the resistors leads.
Finally, it appears they used 16 awg wire. I would have been happier with something bigger, like 14awg.

title: Motion detection range is short (25ft), but works well inside that.
text:
*7 month update
Still on the original batteries with fairly high traffic, but I've pretty much got the rest of the house and yard covered with wyze cams.

The one advantage that blink has over wyze is that it can be used for alexa routines which turn things off if no motion is detected for a certain amount of time.

If they ever add continuous recording when wired, or key support, they could fill a bigger niche, but the wyze v3 is currently better in every way, unless you can't run wires.

The biggest reason i still havent sold these is that all cameras occasionally disconnect from WiFi and stop sending notifications, and having 2 different systems helps mitigate this risk.

*Update
I'm going ahead with 4 star at this point. After moving the cameras down off the soffits to around 10' high on the walls, they do meet the 25' range specified in the FAQs page. This ad the customer support received earns a slightly grudging 4 star. Just be aware of the limitations.

I've added a couple screenshots with red lines added to illustrate where they pick me up in a meandering walk to the entrances.

*Update
bumped to 3-star, as it's more a description ommission than a product issue*
I was contacted by customer support after writing my original review and doing a bit of research myself. Apparently the motion detection only has about a 25 ft range, so if you're like me and want to overlook a large area, these are not for you unless you get several cameras and mount them low. I wish this had been mentioned in the product details.

It should be noted that the reason the motion detection range is so short compared with wyze, is that it uses an infrared sensor for primary motion detection. This is probably more reliable for outdoor and low light, but again, would have been nice to see on the product details.

So, I'll be moving the cameras down from our 18' soffits and adding more cameras in the future. If they work significantly better lower, I'll bump the rating accordingly.

Hopefully at some point in the near future blink adds continuous recording with event clips for those of us willing to hardwire power, and with local storage provided by the new sync mod 2. This would make the motion detection range much less of an issue.

*Original 2-star review*
Motion detection leaves a lot to be desired vs wyze.

I've had this up for 2 days and get plenty of alerts for shadows and bugs, but when my wife pulls into the driveway, opens the gate, and walks 30 feet to the door before it picks up motion??

Also, it picks up my dogs every time they use the dog door, despite the zone being set to inactive. Back camera allowed me to walk around the backyard, then up 10 steps directly in front of the camera before picking motion up as I opened the screen door.

The attached photo is at max resolution and was the start of the motion clip.

At least with wyze I get constant recording to local storage, so I can review the preceding events when I get an alert like this.

Maybe the motion detection works better if closer up and not covering a large area, but this is awful.

title: Only Ones Advertised as Fireproof!
text:

We recently had a rival brand catch fire from an electrical fluctuation during a bad thunderstorm and it burned a substantial hole in the rug and filled our home office with acrid smoke! FORTUNATELY we were home at the time and able to quickly put out the fire.

These Echogear units also have a high joule rating, a light to alert you when your joules have been expended and your electronics no longer have surge protection, and sliding tabs to cover unused outlets (helps keep dust out of outlets . . .another potential fire hazard).

P.S. We have now placed our 4 new surge protectors on our marble window sills, no longer placing them on any surface that can possibly burn. I highly recommend purchasing marble or ceramic tiles to place under your surge protectors in you have them on carpeting.

title: Good for boat navigation with iPad
text:
I bought this to use with a WiFi-only iPad on which I am running Navionics for boat navigation. I recently sailed from Miami to Gulfport, MS both across parts of the Gulf and the ICW. This unit paired seamlessly with the iPad and was accurate enough for my use. I mounted it at my helm with some doublesided Velcro and even under the bimini I had no reception issues.

It isn’t waterproof or maybe even water resistant so I need to rig up some sort of waterproof case for it that won’t reduce reception. Otherwise no issues. Battery life was pretty good - sometimes 12 hours. Usually 8-10. But there is no real battery meter so I would just charge it up with a battery pack while still using it when the low battery light started to flash.

This plus a WiFi iPad made for a good primary nav setup for my 34’ sailboat. That said I also bought an android tablet as my backup, which comes with built in GPS, and it worked great too (see my other reviews). I’m partial to the build quality of Apple products and for something I was literally trusting the existential safety of myself and my boat with I used the apple + garmin combo and can recommend it. That said, you can buy three android tablets for the price of one apple+garmin and have redundancies. But I digress. This Garmin is a good product.

title: Flimsy and power-hungry
text:
First, I was given this product in return for my impartial and honest review. Thank you, Leadsail. Note that this review is for the "Silent Click Wireless Computer Mouse, 2.4G Portable Slim Cordless Mouse" : it has a translucent red shell. Leadsail sells a number of mice, and apparently all the reviews are mixed together.

I am a mouse fanatic. I spend a lot of time on the PC, and between typing and clicking, those are two of the most important ergonomic devices needed. But I'm not averse to saving money on something that works. This, I'm not so sure about.

Minus:
• I have fairly large hands... at least long fingers. This sits a bit too low for me, like my hand is flat to the desk. I simply think I prefer a taller mouse, that allows me to cup my hand.
• The manual refers to turning it off when not using to save power. That's unusual for mice anymore, since they power-down automagically when not being used. But this one randomly (?) and frequently lights up inside, for reasons unknown, which must use some power. It's also distracting. See photos.
• It feels cheap and flimsy.
• It often stalls, provoking a jerky response. Now I must admit that my cave is a mess, lots of electronics, three different computers having all sorts of stuff. But the USB receiver is a mere two feet line-of-sight, only the keyboard between them. I don't think the distance is an issue. But maybe the interference of other devices is. Your results may vary.
• The manual.

Plus:
• I really like the center button that allows for three DPI changes on-the-fly. Sometimes you just prefer precision.
• It is quiet. And I have used loud mice, especially the scroll wheel, which drives me crazy.
• The buttons' tactile response is suitable.

Take away: For $13 it's a functional, quiet mouse. Just buy rechargeable AA batteries. And don't let all that flashing bother you.

I will preface this by saying we have a lot of smart hone devices, motion and cameras and smart switches so I am proficient in installing and setting up things like this. We purchased this to use as a baby monitor in our toddlers room.

The camera was very quick and easy to set up, however it came with no instructions. Because I have set up a similar camera I was able to quickly figure it out but this would be confusing for many people.

It comes with an adhesive circle for mounting to the wall. Rather than be stuck ripping it off the wall in order to unplug it or re-pair, I attached it with Velcro command strips.
The camera is crystal clear, with great night vision. I am very happy with the picture. It has great functions, record, screenshot, intercom, everything you would need.

The sound is another story. I cannot understand anything that comes through the microphone on my phone. The audio coming out of the camera is slightly better.

So the TLDR version is, no instructions, short cord, no AC plug, sound is terrible, picture is awesome. If that suits your needs, then it’s a good deal. I’m not super happy about the sound but since I’ve already got it installed and for the price, it’s not worth the hassle to take it down.

title: Great little computer; j4105 CPU has enough power
text:
Got this AWOW NV41 (not the stick) for kicks -- something to try and I'm very satisfied. I wanted a dedicated small music player PC for a DIY preamp with a built-in USB/DAC to see how it would perform. As a music player this has plenty of CPU capacity -- running at around 0.8GHz most the time (using TaskManager) with only Foobar2000 running. It streamed music from a couple of sites just fine.

It can certainly perform well with software such as an office suite. I installed Libre Office and the Writer worked well during my short test.

For kicks I changed the boot drive to a M.2 WD 250GB, copying the original boot device and merging the unused portion with AOMEI Partition Assistant. Many trial or free software either doesn't merge partitions or won't merge partitions unless adjacent. Many will copy the boot drive. As another reviewer wrote and I concur, can easily select the boot device in BIOS - press DEL key on boot up, go to Boot on the menu, down to the first boot device and hit return to select your new device - save and exit.

Other features
RAM: at 4GB installed 3.7GB is available and with just Foobar running (and TaskManager) this machine used about 2GB. So for me 4GB is the minimum. OS: came with Windows 10 Pro installed; I wasn't certain as different places on Amazon such as descriptions and comparisons just showed Windows 10; the AWOW site showed Win10Pro. Would Windows Home Edition use less RAM so 2GB as many sticks have would work without paging to SSD? I don't know. I want the Pro version for Remote Desktop and ability to control the music player from my tablet or phone. SSD: 64GB is needed or larger because around 23GB is used just for Windows (and Foobar which is tiny) so not much is left if you had a 32GB SSD. I think 64GB is good for many dedicated uses. 2.5" SSD -- I installed a 1TB San Disk for data (I checked the thickness spec) and it was super easy to install as was the M.2 SSD. I just had to format it and it was available. Either of these formats work well for extra storage just watch the type of M.2 keying you get. My use of WiFi was at about 40ft and it worked very well for internet access. I used the Ethernet connection for copying my data which was much faster than (my) WIFI.

I got this for around $170 on Amazon plus the cost of the two SSD's. The AWOW NV41S stick PC was my next choice being smaller but more $$$ and with just SD memory expansion I like this NV41. The j4105 CPU on comparisons sites shows it performing quite well. For a basic music player the Atom would do fine if other aspects are met (such as 4GB RAM and for me 250GB SD which many less expensive sticks don't support). Other features not mentioned haven't been used yet (other than the type A USB ports which all worked).

Documentation: NONE was received. I didn't look on the AWOW site for a manual. I found it worked when I plugged in a wireless keyboard-mouse and HDMI display. The power adapter comes with three plugs -- you have to slide a cover off and slide the connection plug you need on and slide the lock in place. Easy enough.

Other ratings: I didn't have a need to contact tech support and I don't really care about energy efficiency with regard to this type of product so I didn't rate these aspects. As for gaming -- I'm not a gamer but understand some people have very powerful machines for gaming. This isn't one of those machines and cannot comment on this aspect.

title: Outdated product, time to retire.
text:
This product is not even good if you want to have this feel of 2010. Wi-Fi protocols 802.11 G and N can’t coexist with the newest AC/AD and AF. These bands cause interference. Channel width for Wireless G and N is 40 MHz vs AC 80 MHz in fact AC itself capable of 1.5 GB/s is an outdated protocol but is what everybody is using. G and N networks drop your bandwidth to 10% of subscribed speed 300MB/s to 30MB/s
Additionally we have to look at security protocols. Newest security protocol is WPA3. This router supports Wired Equivalent Protocol (WEP) an easily hackable WiFi security started in 1999 and abandoned in 2004 apparently not by Netgear that put this in a product 6 years later and still sell it 10 years later.
This is a good product for museums or collectors of old technology. Shouldn’t be your next router.
Amazon, Netgear are you serious?

I was pleased when I put this little scope together and used it. I've been using a small stereo dissecting scope for years but needed a camera, so I tried this little digital scope. For the low magnification I need it's fine, it's not so good at the extreme 1200X it claims, but it's usable at the higher magnification. It may be a plus that the rig has a rechargeable battery that will power the lamps and the display for at least an hour or so without it being plugged in.

The focus is a little bit touchy to use, is not a knob with a rack and pinion like an ordinary scope, is a knurled ring that's turned directly. And it's not a true 'zoom' scope as advertised since it needs to be refocused when the head is moved up or down to adjust the magnification.

But, it can be focused sharply and it does have adjustable magnification. I believe it's excellent value for somebody who wants to get good video or photos of biological samples, or the coins in the headline.

It didn't work so well for what I need to do this time, which is brushing through samples in a Petri dish looking for microscopic eggs and hatchling worms. I'm spoiled by years of working with a stereo scope and find it's much easier using tools with the stereo and betterdepth of field of an optical scope. I bought the trinocular stereo zoom scope and camera I've always wanted. I had to pay nearly $600+ for that rig.

Of course the new scope with binocular stereo and big optics looks and feels better. But, for about $100 I don't think this little scope can be beat for good value if you don't need stereo vision.

I sold this scope on eBay after using it for a few days, added an SD card to it, and got back $80 from the happy buyer. It was worth the $20 bucks to see that an inexpensive, digital scope can be this good.

I love my new, huge, trinocular dissecting scope that puts the binoculars right at eye level and has an 18 MegaPixel camera. And, I like this little digital scope fine, for 1/6th the price.

I'd suggest it's an excellent scope for somebody in school or for somebody with a hobby that doesn't need stereo. It's ideally suited as the 'coin microscope' it's advertised as, is also fine for anything that needs looking at.

text:
This is a great, portable SSD. Fast transfers, good support, good price point. I swapped over from HDD after having a really bad crash which lost me all my data. Many people suggested I get an SSD, and being a broke-ass college student this one was in my price-range and large enough to hold all my files (I'm a designer and illustrator so I've got lots of Photoshop, After Effects and Illustrator projects).

At first I was very happy with my SSD. I don't run programs off it, I just use it to save backups of projects and transfer files back and forth as my main laptop at the moment has very little memory. But after a while I've had serious issues with it getting way too hot, to the point where I'm concerned about it crashing or straight up melting (which has happened to me before).

I've got a 1tb and if I just leave it plugged into my computer, not transferring data or anything it will get VERY hot. Like almost too hot to touch. I haven't had any crashes, YET. But I'm very wary now when I use it. I'm already shopping again for a new SSD, and just use this one as an emergency backup. I usually transfer my files, and unplug it immediately before it can get too hot.

Smaller and cheaper isn't always better so if you do purchase this just be careful of overheating. I would caution people that they shouldn't just leave it plugged in for extended amounts of time. Especially if you've plugged in the SSD on the same side as the charging port. I did this and it overheated even faster. Not sure if I'm just stupid for doing this or if this is a genuine problem. I do have an older Macbook Air so maybe that contributes, not sure. But the thing was like scolding hot after and I quickly ejected it and set it in front of my desk fan to help it cool off.

title: Buyer beware
text:
My mom wanted a wow computer so we got it for her back in 2017. The first computer had to be sent back because after a few months it started typing backwards! The replacement did the same thing. Eventually that problem went away but there’s always a new problem to take its place. It is a closed operating system that they update on their end and push out to all of the computers. So something that might have been stable one day all of a sudden starts malfunctioning the next. My mom has been without incoming email for over a month (June 2020) because Comcast changed some security settings and the wow computer people have not been able to figure out how to change the code on their end to make the email program work. It is now July and they still have not fixed it. She now has to go to the web and into Comcast website to read her emails as a work around. She’s 85 years old, teaching her new things is difficult.

The computer itself is cheap. The keyboard and mouse are lightweight plastic junk. The keyboard is very clunky and hard to type on.

Customer service is basically nice. Located here in the US (which is an aspect we like. No foreign accents to confuse my mom Who is hard of hearing) but to be without email for over a month and to just be told “we are working on it” is not enough. In 2019 I was told they only had 5 coders who could work on issues. Recently I was told they had “maybe 15”. This is a small company and cannot be compared to the likes of apple or windows. The idea is a noble one. To create a computer that is easy for seniors. But the execution fell short. Buyer beware.

title: Excellent value for the money!
text:
I'm on the second week now of using the Lenovo C330 convertible Chromebook (there are multiple models on the site under C330 so I'm specifying it is the model with 4GB RAM, 64GB SSD, MediaTek MT8173C processor). I needed to replace my 9 year old Macbook Pro that was an excellent machine but just couldn't handle modern computing needs. However, I have a desktop for more intense computing needs, so I really didn't want to spend $1000+ on a new MacBook to browse the web, watch YouTube videos, read eBooks, watch Netflix etc in the evening. Cheap laptops in the sub $350 range are frankly almost all junk, so I wasn't really interested in buying one of those either. I don't want a tablet because I want a keyboard and I like to lie flat in bed and that's just not convenient.

Enter the Chromebook! So far, this has been an impressive solution for the purchase price of $231. Of course, Chromebooks have a variety of hardware and you need to do your homework to get the best experience. For about $50 more than lesser Chrombooks, this is an ideal middle ground solution. Within its comparable price range, the MediaTek MT8173C processor scores at the top as far as processing speed. Coupled with 4GB DDR3 RAM and a 64 GB SSD for boot speed, plus how lightweight of an OS ChromeOS is, this is a very well performing little machine for the price. Web browsing is snappy, YouTube loads very quickly and the Google Play store gives you access to all the apps you need. So far, all apps have loaded without any issues and function well. The battery life is remarkable - I've gotten 13-14 hours of use from it and still had 15% when I finally plugged it in. ChromeOS is super easy to learn/user friendly and reminds me of the user experience of a phone/tablet.

NOW - this machine is not a few things. It doesn't have a super high resolution screen, but it's a small screen, so it's not bad, but if you're used to a Retina screen it will be a bit lower in quality. It is fine and perfectly functional, but not exceptional, as a tablet (not the best touch screen response and obviously heavier than normal tablets and ChromeOS isn't as optimized for touch screen use compared to phone/tablet operating systems - think things like bigger front/back/X buttons - those aren't as prevalent on ChromeOS). The keypad is nice and sensitive but the click is loud. Printing is probably a pain but I have a desktop for that, so I don't care. So far, those are really the only cons I have found to this machine, but the pros far outweigh and you need to be realistic about features vs. price. It does a lot of things really well at the current list price of $251. It is not a $1000 laptop and you simply can't expect $1000 features from it.

I'm very glad I spent the extra money for this over the sub-$200 Chromebooks with lower quality hardware and no convertible/touch screens. The convertible/touch really makes it fun to use.

So, in summary: If you just need a machine to do run of the mill browsing, streaming, etc I think this is an almost perfect solution and an excellent value for the money.

title: If you have a 4K display and want resolutions higher than 1080 @ 60Hz, don't get this
text:
So... there's "4K" and then there's actual 4K.

This device is continuously using your CPU to re-render your screen to a 4K display... no wonder why it's capped at 1080...

Even then, say you LOVE 4K at 1080 (I could see why you do)... if you are used to having your windows be dragged and feel like butter because they are to be so smooth at 4K@60Hz... forget about this device... it lags worse than Fortnite over dial-up. You'll be sorely disappointed...

I have a 2020 13" MacBook Pro and a 24" 4K Dell Display... if it makes you nervous when you install a device that warns you to allow it to record your screen (because it needs to pipe it to the attached monitor), then don't get it (saving you the pain). The same MacBook got hooked to a CalDigit TB3 dock and just worked. No drivers, no capped resolutions at 1080... and bonus (ding ding ding ding) it charges your Mac while attached to it.

If you want a dock that powers your Mac, that supports higher than 1080 @ 60Hz, and doesn't require you to install "drivers" so it can happily record your screen (and hopefully only does that with such recordings)... don't get this device.

Took me longer to plug it in than to have it boxed and ready to go back where it came from.

title: Momentum 3: Noise cancelation, pressure feeling, sound quality, fit, etc
text:
According to most professional reviews I've read (more than a dozen), these aren't the best in noise canceling, though a couple reviewers don't notice a difference with the best Sony or Bose, and they're improved over the Momentum 2.

BUT some prefer the sound of the Sennheisers enough to more than make up for potential differences in noise cancelation. I haven't heard the others, but I do love the sound of these and find the noise suppression good enough.

The sound (also reportedly improved over the 2) is clear and clean, detailed, with powerful, extended bass. The top end is handled in a way that makes them easy to listen to at any volume, even with material that isn't well recorded. That's a useful feature in phones sometimes used for resting. And the frequency balance can be (roughly) adjusted with the app.

Along with my other comments I'm going to include a few not-very-technical explanations of technical points for those who may want them.

These are Bluetooth 5 compliant (backward compatible) and can use aptX, aptX Low Latency, AAC, and SBC codecs for high quality sound and lack of delay.

Noise canceling

According to an engineer who has worked on it (quoted at soundstagesolo), standard active noise-canceling (ANC) works for low and low-midrange frequencies, below 1kHz. Noise isolation for upper-mids and highs, he says, is passive, i.e. good sound insulation.

That may be why these phones cancel low-frequency noise impressively well, but higher frequencies somewhat less.

In the default max cancellation mode, the sound from my TV's good external speakers is reduced from loud and full to something like a cell phone speaker several feet away, still quite audible if I don't have anything playing on the headphones. Similarly, standing next to a highway, traffic noise is nearly eliminated in the lows but still clearly audible, if much quieter, higher up.

There's an anti-pressure ANC mode (accessed via the app) that's supposed to prevent the feeling of pressure in the ears some people experience with ANC (more below). It sounds similar to the max mode but with a little more mid-frequency sound coming through.

And there's an anti-wind mode. It cuts lower-pitched wind noise better than the max mode, though some higher-pitched whistling sounds get through with both. For other kinds of noise it's less effective.

(No) pressure

According to the sound engineer, an abrupt transition between active and passive cancelation around 1kHz causes some people to feel a pressure sensation in their ears, which can be mild to painful. Many others don't feel it. (Theory and measurements suggest there isn't any change in pressure; it may be sound traits the brain interprets as pressure.)

So there may be a tradeoff between cancelation and feeling pressure. The headphones with the maximum canceling right up to near 1kHz may cause the most pressure sensation. Those that taper off the ANC more gradually, and consequently let more sound in leading up to 1kHz, seem to cause less trouble.

That may be why the anti-pressure mode on these lets more midrange sound in.

But even the max mode seems not to bother people. I haven't seen any reports of people feeling pressure in the ears with the ANC on these headphones.

Hear the Beard (sound quality)

That's Dusty Hill's Beard. These are a bassist's dream, with strong extended bass, well into subwoofer range. (No loss of power at 20Hz, usually considered the lower limit of hearing. Sennheiser claims a remarkable 6Hz-22kHz range.) And it's clean and tight. I always evaluate headphones with a set of songs I know well, including ZZ Top's "I Thank You," which has a prominent bass line from Mr. Hill. On these phones it throbs and pulses like with no others I've tried, but it's still in control, doesn't muddy up the song.

The extended bass is especially satisfying with pipe organ music, where the pedal work is often only hinted at with other headphones. These rumble and growl as they should.

It handles even the deepest rap beats with ease.

Some people (not me) find the bass too much. They might want to use the EQ function (see below).

The rest of the frequency spectrum is also clean, detailed, with good separation and soundstage. The top is lively but not hot. Sibilants aren't harsh, hi-hats sound natural. Like most headphones, they roll off some of the very highest sounds between 10-20kHz, some of which most of us can't hear anyway. That's generally for the best. These are more relaxed and less fatiguing than phones that don't roll off the very top.

There's no distortion at extreme volume. They can get louder than I can listen to with most inputs, and no source I've tried has been too quiet to get the volume I want.

EQ

There's an equalizer function in the app. It doesn't allow fine control over any portion of the frequency range, but you can move a dot that adjusts the frequency-response curve to boost or lessen either or both ends or the middle. It's flexible and effective in a broad way, and easy enough. Once you adjust it, it stays that way until you change it.

ANC sound quality

ANC presents challenges for sound quality that some phones don't overcome well. With these the effect is small, usually unnoticeable even in a quiet environment. If I'm paying close attention, these sometimes sound a little more open and airy with ANC off.

Isolation

The closed design with thick ear pads that seal well means better isolation from others hearing what you're listening to, though they can still hear a little if they're close in.

Transparent mode

There's a button on the headphones for this. It's not quite like taking the phones off, but it's close enough to clearly hear others talking, TV, or whatever. Via the app you can set it so music stops in transparent mode, which is the default, or keeps going.

Bluetooth

Bluetooth connectivity is fine with my 2016 MacBook Pro, not so great with my 2011 MBP, where there's breakup and pausing after a while. With the latter, which I only use for sports video streaming (17"), I use the cable instead with no trouble.

You can connect to two devices at once.

Wired

These come with a cable to use with a regular 1/8" (3.5mm) headphone jack. For some music it sounds even better, a little cleaner and more open still. Mostly the sound is very similar as long as the power is on.

With the headphones powered off (open while pushing the middle button), the sound isn't as good in my experience, but they're still usable that way in a pinch.

Bluetooth is automatically disabled when plugged in, so you can't take or make calls. You can't use the music controls either. But you can still use ANC as long as the battery has power. If no battery power, you can still listen without ANC.

Getting the plug in right on the ear cup was more difficult than it should be at first, but not hard now. You have to line up a tiny notch on the plug with a tiny protrusion on the jack and then push in and twist clockwise. The good part is that it stays in very securely.

For some setups you can also get audio via the USB cable, though my Mac doesn't recognize it for that.

Fit, physical comfort

On my average-size male head the ear cups pressed tightly at first, but after some use and some very gentle headband stretching they became very comfortable. You can speed that up by keeping the ear cups spread across something the size of or a little larger than your head overnight. You need them to remain snug, though, so that they'll seal well.

The ear pads are luxurious, supple leather over soft padding. They're very deep, so even though my ears stick out they don't get mashed down as they do with most headphones.

The ear pads get a good seal with glasses. I've worn these for hours at a time without any discomfort from glasses.

The headband has the same supple leather but with less padding, about 1/4". The padding is a little over an inch wide at the top, divided into two ridges that run the length of the headband, probably cooler that way. As with most headphones, after a while I get a pain at the crown of my head and need to move the headband for a second, and then it's comfortable again.

At just under 11 ounces these are 0.9 ounces heavier than Sony's WH-1000MX3 and 1.6 ounces more than Bose's 700.

Buttons

I'm not wild about touchpad controls on headphones, which tend to do things I don't want, so I'm glad these have buttons. They're easy to use, though it takes a little homework to learn all the ways to use them.

There's one for ANC on/off and transparent mode.

There are two for volume up and down and mic muting.

Between the volume buttons is a "multifunction" button that controls music playback, phone functions, battery check, and opening without turning on.

And there's a voice assistant button that also handles pairing and flight mode (Bluetooth off).

There's no on/off button. They turn on when you open them, and go off when you close them. You can open them without turning them on by holding down the multi-function button while opening.

Call quality

I don't use these for calls, but I've noticed the professional reviews generally think they're good, with clear sound on both ends. A couple have found it sounds clear but a little distant to those on the other end.

Battery life

At 13-17 hours per charge with Bluetooth and ANC on (according to various tests), these don't offer as much as the nearest competitors, or the Momentum 2.

You can quick-charge these for 10 minutes to get another 1-1/2 hours of use. It's 3 hours for a full charge.

Unlike many competitors, you can still use these while they're charging.

You can also use them without the battery like normal wired headphones, though you lose the ANC if the battery's dead.

The battery isn't user replaceable, which is sadly the usual these days. Sennheiser says they'll replace it for a fee.

A USB-C charging cable is included, with a USB-A adapter.

Other points

There's a Smart Pause feature that pauses music when you take the phones (or right ear cup) off. It can also take a call when you put the phones on, mute it when you take them off, and resume when you put them back on. Some people have found it may pause/mute if they turn their heads a certain way or even yawn. I turned it off in the app, as I usually don't want pausing.

As mentioned above, you can open these without powering them on, by pushing the middle button while opening.

TILE compliant, if you want to set up that app so you can find these when you lose them.

NFC compliant.

The app has been stable on my Android phone, but it doesn't always show the battery level.

The case is nice but bulkier than it needs to be. I think I'll use a pouch instead.

There are voice and tone prompts. You can turn either or both off with the app.

There's a fairly detailed online manual.

Warranty is two years, doesn't cover batteries or ear cushions (also replaceable).

Designed and engineered in Germany, assembled in Romania.

title: An Absolute Joy to Use
text:
I was looking to change things up from my old D3100. Initially I figured full frame was the way to go for an upgrade on account of what so may blogs, videos, influencers, and forums had said; much to my suprise, I ended up heading in almost the exact opposite direction when it comes to camera philosophy, and I couldn't be happier about it.
Taking my time, I decided to list out what I was looking for in a camera. I have always been rather inspired with the work of Edward Weston and other members of f.64, therefore I decided that seeking out extremely shallow depth of field was not important. I had been very much enjoying shooting on an old Canon AE-1, particularly the form factor and portability of that system. I don't shoot billboard campaigns or crop my photos excessively, therefore I had no need for extra high resolution. I also don't find myself shooting weddings or action in low light very often, so high ISO performance fell off as a need. Against all odds, this list of requirements lined up pretty well with the Micro 4/3 landscape. After more research and refining of my list of needs/wants, it came down to either an E-M5 II or an E-M10 III. The weather sealing and hi-res shot mode on the E-M5 ultimately swung my decision. I paired it with the Panasonic 25mm 1.7 and the Olympus 40-150mm and haven't looked back!
I recently took my kit on a trip to the Channel Islands and it performed superbly. Very compact and easy to hike around with while simultaneously delivering great images. As a bonus, I was able to pick up an adapter to use my old Canon FD lenses with my Olympus, which works surprisingly well. title: Works Great in Lenovo E540 .
text:
I had 4GB of RAM in my Thinkpad laptop a Lenovo E540 so 16GB should be a great improvement right? I understand 16GB is the max for the E540 so I got 2 of the Patriot SODIMMs.
Easy to install. Remove battery and the 3 captured screws on the back and remove cover to access the SODIMM slots.
There are 2 SODIMM slots in the E540 that actually overlap and they lay at a low angle to the motherboard.
I only had 1 4GB SODIMM installed.
Push aside the guide/lever and the old RAM SODIMM pops right out.
Push inn the new RAM, bottom slot first, into the socket at an angle until it seats in the socket then push down on it for the retainers to snap into place. Repeat for the 2nd RAM card on top.
After power up I checked the system config and now I have 15.7 GB "Usable".
I dont know how to quantify any performance improvement but Im hoping somethings are a lot faster but at least I know there is 16GB working RAM.
When I first I powered up the, Windows Security Essentials got a little panicky as it asked to be manually started so must have been something to do with the new RAM.
So if you were wondering if this RAM works in the Lenovo E540 its a big YES!

I would still recommend it for those that really enjoy the iOS iPad interface and experience. However, for $300, if you are happy with your laptop, then I would say don’t bother.

title: Great Comfort, Great Value, Poor Convenience
text:
I took the risk in buying this headset that has seemingly zero support and not a big crowd that actually owns it. Every article I could find on the thing was mostly just talking about the Kickstarter for it. I only managed to find two videos of people doing a mic test and the only other video was some crazy audiophile crapping on this headset because it's not as good as his other $300 headsets (no duh??). After using it now for two days I can say there are some things that I wish I would've known before buying this as they would've made me not buy it.

First off, the mic quality is both good and bad. It's weird to say it that way but it's true. The mic is clear and crisp, but it lacks any actual depth. I feel this is in part due to the fact that the "stereoscopic" mic doesn't come out more than an inch from the actual headset itself and it stays behind the corner of your mouth so the audio pickup is very indirect. There is no boost settings for this mic either and it has a large amount of static electrical noise which is quite annoying for a headset that so generously boasts that it has "electrical noise cancellation". There is built in toggle-able noise cancellation but don't bother with it because the moment you turn it on the mic goes from "Okay this is a fairly decent mic!" to "Wow this sounds like Logitech..." and for those of you with some experience of Logitechs headsets you know what I mean. That tinny, nasty, compressed sound that Logitech just can't seem to fix in any of their headsets. Overall, the mic quality is good but it gets shot down by the fact that the "TELESCOPIC" mic won't go past the side of your cheek and a lack of good noise cancellation.

The next thing that isn't so clear is the driver setup for this. The manual doesn't do much justice for telling you what you need to do and it wasn't until after struggling for two hours to fix the sound that I found out the headset uses a C-Media driver / software combo that introduces a few useful settings for everything except your mic. In the software there is a generous amount of options to enhance your listening experience. There is a built in equalizer and the headset can go up to 24B/98000HZ which with the 53mm drivers it is a fantastic listening experience after tweaking some things. You'll find the headset naturally leans towards the bass side of the spectrum and lacks any real natural treble sounds. So the EQ comes into play for that. The digital surround sound works really well for a headset. In all honesty, for $50 this headset is a good deal. It has a good balance of mic quality and audio quality.

For the convenience side of things... where do I start? The folding headphones are great if you travel a-lot and are continuously moving your working location around BUT for working at a stationary position (like at home, or at work for extended periods of time) the folding headphones are a pain the hakuna-matatas. You have to fumble with them to put them back on and they roll around in your fingers, makes it a bit of an unnecessary hassle to put them on. The braided cable is very itchy and feels more like a hard plastic than anything. So be warned, don't roll the cable up or it's gonna stay like that forever. As previously mentioned, be ready to install a driver software and tinker with the audio for a good while. The mic also by default is enabled with Studio input instead of Mono and will only record the Left Track at first. So be ready to change that as well. I feel this is not necessary for a gaming headset.

So overall, it's a great value and a unique style. The mic is good but has limiting factors.

I don't leave many reviews, but this thing is very impressive for how much they're charging for it...exceptionally so. The screen is big enough that there's no issue playing even text-heavy RPGs like Chrono Trigger or Final Fantasy __. The speakers aren't amazing, but get the job done. The Game HAT board also has four easy-to-miss buttons on one side that give you a nice menu to adjust brightness, contrast, saturation, volume, etc., making it easy to tweak those settings without having to mess with the complicated RetroPie DOS menus.

While it doesn't come with a battery, I was able to find one online and get it installed no problem. The battery life is decent, and there are indicator lights on the Game HAT board for 25, 50, 75, and 100% battery life, so you know if you need to charge it soon (you can also play as you charge if you need to).

As someone without a ton of free time, it's amazing for me to be able to pick this up and play whenever I have a few minutes. I absolutely love it. Great product.

title: Decent Monitor
text:
There are pros and cons to this monitor. The CV27F comes very well packed and is easily unpacked from its packaging. Included are 3 different types of cords to supply power to the monitor (to accommodate other countries). Also included are a DP cable, an HDMI cable, and the USB pass-through so that the USB ports can be utilized that are built into the monitor. This cable is also required to use the Sidekick software that allows you to control everything about this monitor with your mouse and keyboard so that you do not have to use the physical control on the monitor itself. Its stand goes on quite easily, and the stand is much lighter than the one than came with the AD27QD. This monitor can also be easily mounted to a desk or wall mount.

Those are the pro's for this monitor. The cons however only come into play if you are used to using a monitor with a 1440 resolution. If that is the case, you are not going to be happy with this one and I strongly suggest that you pay the little extra and choose the CV27Q instead. This monitor has 1080p resolution on a VA panel. Coming from 1440's with IPS panels and even running two beside it (the AD27QD and the PG328Q), the difference is immediate and in your face. The colors are washed out on the CV27F (even setting the presets on both Aorus monitors to the exact same thing) and the details in what you are viewing are completely lost when comparing the exact same picture or video, side by side on the AD27Q. For me, I think its both the resolution and panel type that I am used to that has me seeing this monitor the way that I do.

If you have always used 1080p monitors with VA panels, that you will definitely love this monitor with its features. But, 1440 and IPS have always been your playground.... try to see this one in person before making the decision to purchase.

title: Bought 2 - Both were Faulty and had to be Returned
text:
Based on other reviews, I bought two of these speakers, so that we could have 1 upstairs and 1 downstairs.

I immediately plugged them into an outlet to charge. I wasn't sure when they were charged because there is an indicator light, but it was flashing, then another time later was solid red, and at other times was not on at all.
I checked the directions, but they were confusing. In one sentence it says "The red light of charging indicator are always on and the screen battery icon stops blinking to indicate that the battery is full." But the very next sentence says, "(Note: the screen is not lit and the charging light is long in the state of shutdown.)" What?!?

Anyhow, I left them charging until they stopped blinking. Neither one gave the verbal "low battery, please charge", when I turned them on, so I'm fairly certain they were successfully charged.

FIRST SPEAKER
I connected one speaker to a phone via bluetooth, which was very simple to connect. The sound was awesome and for a couple hours I was very happy with the speaker.

Then the phone battery started dying so I put it on a charger, and thought maybe the speaker could use a charge as well, but when I plugged it in, the battery indicator did not blink so I took it back off, assuming it was still charged. Since this was advertised to last 8 or 9 hours, I figured it was still good, because I'd only been playing it for 2 or 3 hours, and the directions say that it'll give a verbal warning, and it didn't.

The phone is old and I had trouble getting it to charge and it died. I immediately went to turn off the speaker, but it had the word "blue" displayed and would not power off.
No matter what buttons I pushed or held, the speaker did not respond. I left it over night and tried the next morning, it still displayed "blue".
I walked through trying to reset it with an Amazon customer rep, but the speaker remained unresponsive - not even a blink. He sent me a link to notify the seller, but they responded with: hold down the power button, use the little reset hole, and try a different power cord. These had already been tried - so this speaker is a brick that does nothing but display "blue" on the screen.

SECOND SPEAKER
Now I'm a bit concerned and decide to try the second speaker. Our original intent was to put a mini SD card in the speakers so we wouldn't have to run the battery dead on our phones.

I tried to put the card into the slot and noticed that it was a weird, sloppy fit, so I was pretty nervous about the possibility of losing my card inside the speaker. I braved it and was able to click it into place and confirm that I could click it back out. I inserted the card and turned on the speaker, but it ignored the card and requested a bluetooth connection. I went back to the manual and interpreted the confusing instructions to say. Power on first, then insert card. Great, I was going to have to unclick and reclick in the card every time I turned on the speaker. Okay, it's a minor inconvenience, I can deal with that, as long as it plays the music good.

First song starts up and it's excellent, sounds great. I'm happy again; this is what I wanted. The second song comes up, but about halfway through the song, I hear this horrible, intermittent static/scratching sound. "What the...?!"

I'm thinking that there is a glitch in the sound file, so I switch to the next song. Nope, the intermittent static/scratching sound continues. I immediately shut down the speaker and take out my card. I'm done, they both have to be returned.

My advice is to avoid this brand. I got 2 speakers and both had serious, but different, issues within 24 hours of receiving them. One issue could be explained away as an anomaly, both having issues indicates to me that there is something wrong with the manufacturing, quality control, or both.

title: SoundPEATS Strikes Again !  Q12 Plus  BT 5.0 wireless magnetic In-Ear-Monitors 9 hours playtime !
text:
SoundPEATS Q12 Plus
Bluetooth 5.0 & incredible new chip sets to use several codecs on different devices. Connects with little to no effort to 2 devices and stays connected as you go back and forth from music to phone to music to a second phone and back all day long.
Magnetic Wireless In-Ear Buds make it easier not to worry about setting them down & forgetting them, since you never need take them off. Also I found the magnetic buds made it much easier & neater to store in the provided carry case. The fit was interesting at first. It felt a tad strange using these wingtip things and I wasn't sure if they would stay in, since they were so comfortable once on, but I shook my head like a maniac at a headbangers concert for about 30 seconds and ..while I got dizzy as heck..the earbuds didn't move a micron !
I got these at around 2 pm today (it's almost 1 am now) and they have been in since without losing comfort or connection....until I walked into the next room with a few walls, a furnace and refrigerator between the laptop and my Q12 Plus IEMs. Then they cut out a few times before I walked back to the laptop, but they never completely lost the connection...amazing.
These IEMs have an IPX6 rating for being waterproof for sports and outdoor wearing, but I haven't taken them out to the pool or in the rain yet, so I’ll just take them at their word on that.
They say 9 hours of playing time, but I've had much better than that today. It may help that I only had the music up to about 50%, since the bass is quite present in these as compared to the SOUNDPEATS TrueCapsule wireless earphones. I have to say I like both sets for different reasons, but enjoy them both equally :)
It's simply a matter of preference, but SoundPEATS always comes through with flying colors.

title: Needs a few design tweaks
text:
I was pleasantly surprised by the beefy, heavy construction of this lock. However, my initial delight was short lived after discovering two major problems with this lock....

1) The fixing hardware (screws) are TOTALLY INADEQUATE. I expected the installation instructions to tell me to drill an additional hole through the door to secure the two halves of this lock together. Sadly, no provision is made for this and the four tiny screws included only fasten the lower half of the lock bodies together. Even after tightening them securely, the whole lock assembly can twist from the 11-o’clock to the 1-o’clock position. It’s not possible to secure the lock to the door in an upright, plumb orientation.

2) The unit I received refused to operate with four brand new Duracell AA batteries installed. A quick check with a digital voltmeter revealed that the 6.3 volts from the batteries were not reaching the input terminals due to poor workmanship in the battery compartment. I confirmed operation of the lock by connecting a USB charging brick to the emergency backup power input jack and the lock then operated correctly.

It seems like nobody from Turbolock has tried to install this product on an actual door... if they did, they would see that the lock cannot be secured properly together with the hardware included. Also, a quick quality assurance test should have identified a lack of power to the lock CPU from a bad battery compartment harness.

I am requesting a replacement unit be sent to me.

title: Reasonably good sound for price; a bit strident at higher volumes, though
text:
If you're looking for a decent, secondary BT speaker that's affordable to the extent of being disposable if something happens to it, this might be a good choice. I researched a number of different review sites before buying and I'd say that the reviews were pretty much spot on.
1) very affordable for what it is
2) decent, reasonably balanced sound, particularly at lower room volumes
3) strident at higher volumes, especially as music content becomes more complicated. The sound signature changes, too, at higher volumes as the bass disappears and the midranges honk and distort.
4) good choice for traveling, camping, the beach (at low volumes), work, etc.
5) acceptable bass for the price
6) it won't replace your good $150+ BT speaker though

Me, I'm very particular with sound, as a (former) audiophile, so take that into account in my somewhat critical review.

All in all, I'd have no problem recommending it at the $30 +/- price point. Just don't expect it to sound like your $150 BT speaker.
